#5295. Binance Reveals Final Numbers After $6.34 Billion Hack: 100.04% of Shiba Inu (SHIB) Reserves Confirmed

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Binance has published the final results of an unscheduled Proof of Reserves (PoR) report, two weeks after the cryptocurrency exchange lost $6.34 billion in an October hack.

According to Binance, the snapshot was taken on Nov. 12 at 00:00 UTC, and it shows that the exchange fully backs the balances of its clients. Shiba Inu (SHIB) is backed at 100.04%, and the other major assets on the exchange are fully covered as well.

The latest report comes after the Oct. 29 attack, during which hackers stole funds from Binance across ten blockchains in 20 minutes. Among the stolen funds were nearly 500 billion SHIB. After the attack, the exchange took an additional reserve snapshot at Bitcoin block height 975493.

Binance data shows that the net account balances of users stand at 50.67 trillion SHIB, and the exchange holds 50.69 trillion SHIB in its wallets. Of that amount, 50.68 trillion SHIB is held at the addresses of Binance itself, and the remaining 7.46 billion SHIB is held by third-party custodians.

Besides SHIB, the report also shows that the other major cryptocurrencies are fully backed. Compared with the previous check on Nov. 4, the BTC balances of users went up by 0.35% to 687,912 BTC, and the coverage ratio for Bitcoin stands at 100.05%. The ETH balances went up by 1.04% to 3.48 million ETH, and the BNB balances increased by 1.03% to 42.95 million BNB.

Still, the USDT balances of users went down by 3.68% to 24.3 billion USDT. At the same time, the stablecoin has the highest coverage ratio in the report at 104.34%.

Arkham Intelligence data shows that the known wallets of Binance currently hold 58.82 trillion SHIB. That is 5.88% of the total supply of the meme coin, and these tokens are worth $251.16 million. In this context, Binance wallets hold 8.13 trillion SHIB (about $34.7 million) more than the amount shown in the PoR report.

According to Binance, the PoR report only covers the deposits of clients and the coins that the exchange keeps to back them, so the company's own funds are not included in the report. Based on the Arkham data, Binance holds about 16% more SHIB than it owes to its clients.

According to Arkham, Binance is still the third-largest exchange by SHIB holdings. Only the burn address with 410.44 trillion SHIB (or 41.04% of supply), the U.S.-based exchange Coinbase with 74.53 trillion SHIB, and South Korea's Upbit with 64.14 trillion SHIB hold more of the meme coin. Robinhood, Crypto.com and Bithumb come after Binance with 57.12 trillion, 34.95 trillion and 16.74 trillion SHIB, respectively.

Finally, Binance said that the PoR system is still computing the final Merkle Root Hash using zk-SNARKs. After that, users will be able to log into their profiles and check that their balances are included in the overall ledger.

At press time, the price of SHIB stands at $0.00000426.

#5294. Important Ethereum (ETH) Bug Might Be Finally Fixed

One of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub. The patch addresses a vulnerability around the Gloas fork, which could result in some nodes rejecting valid signatures due to a bug in the global pubkey cache.

Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.

The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.

Technically, deposits that are already finalized should give the same validators on every chain, though it is a different story at the fork boundary.

The attacker needs 3 pending deposits just before the fork. The first one is a large top-up for an existing validator. The other two are new keys: A with builder credentials and B with regular validator credentials.

On the canonical chain, the top-up consumes the balance churn, so A and B are processed after the fork. A becomes a builder, and B takes the next validator index.

On the attacker's side chain, the topped-up validator gets slashed before the fork, and its deposit is skipped. This leads to A being processed earlier, essentially taking B's index.

The buggy cache assumed both chains would produce the same validators and imported A's key globally.

At the fork, affected nodes would reject all valid signatures from B on the canonical chain and fork off.

Realistically, the attack is somewhat complicated, as it needs a slashing at the right moment and a side chain, so it's unlikely to happen by accident.

According to the PR, the fix is to only add keys to the global pubkey cache once their activation eligibility epoch is finalized.

A new HeadPubkeys structure also combines keys from the head state and the global cache, so nodes don't miss keys if the chain finalizes without new blocks.

Whether other consensus clients had a similar issue is yet to be confirmed. In other words, the closer Glamsterdam gets, the more edge cases around the fork boundary developers have to catch.

#5293. Protein Startups Are Selling Lots Of Snacks And Drinks. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible

In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.

In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat.

Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat.

The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test.

The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception.

No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert: Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor.

That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food.

Made by: Medici Brands (David parent company).

No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda: The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can.

But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein.

No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn: Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving.

Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose.

No. 4 Mosh: In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver.

The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not.

I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure.

No. 5 Cadootz Crackers: We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed.

For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor.

As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well.

No. 6 Frozen One: For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint.

Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s. But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job.

No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta: We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber.

With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich.

Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami.

#5292. 15 Years Since David Schwartz First Coded XRP Ledger’s Foundation, XRPL’s First Step?

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011, by David Schwartz.

According to the official XRP account on X, the date 11/11/11 marked the beginning of Schwartz's work on what would later support one of the cryptocurrency industry's established payment-focused blockchain networks.

Schwartz, now Ripple CTO Emeritus, was one of three engineers, alongside Jed McCaleb and Arthur Britto, who began developing the XRP Ledger in 2011. The three were inspired by Bitcoin to build an alternative that would address some of its problems, especially in the areas of sustainability and payments.

In June 2012, the XRP Ledger went live. Shortly after Chris Larsen joined the group in September 2012, a company called NewCoin was formed; it soon changed its name to OpenCoin before becoming Ripple. The founders of the XRPL donated 80 billion XRP, the network’s native digital asset, to the company.

Ripple has locked up most of its XRP in escrow, about 55 billion XRP, and releases 1 billion XRP on the first day of every month.

The anniversary on November 11 marks the start of the XRP Ledger’s development, as what began with Schwartz's first code in 2011 eventually morphed into a blockchain network designed to enable value transfers.

November is also a big month for XRP as U.S. spot XRP ETFs celebrate the first anniversary of their landmark launch.Canary Capital’s XRP exchange-traded fund, listed under the ticker XRPC, began trading on November 13, 2025, and is the first spot XRP ETF on a U.S. exchange.

In upgrade news, XRPL version 3.5.0 is scheduled for December 3, 2026. This release includes only improvements and fixes, including a permanent fix for occasional slow ledger close times.

#5291. The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Agentic AI And Infrastructure Are Still On A Roll

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

It was another big week for AI-related startup financings. Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI for R&D, led the pack with a $1 billion series A, followed by Mercor, which secured $750 million to connect AI developers with human experts.

Overall, the vast majority of this week’s largest rounds were AI-related, though we did see some biotech, fintech and enterprise software in the mix.

1. Mirendil, $1B, AI for R&D: Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI technology for research and development, secured $1 billion in a Series A funding. Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the San Francisco-based startup.

2. Mercor, $750M, human-led AI training: Mercor, a platform that connects AI developers with human experts for model training and evaluation, raised $750 million in Series D funding. The round, backed by a long list of venture investors, set a $20 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company, which was founded less than four years ago.

3. Torus, $500M, AI infrastructure: Salt Lake City-based Torus, a manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced a $500 million growth financing led by Magnetar Capital. It also introduced a product called Foundry, described as modular AI infrastructure for inference compute.

4. (tied) Path Robotics, $300M, AI for manufacturing: Path Robotics, a developer of physical AI technology for robotics and manufacturing, with initial expertise in welding, picked up $300 million in Series E financing. Georgian led the round, which set a $2.45 billion valuation for the Columbus, Ohio-based company.

4. (tied) LangChain, $300M, agentic AI: LangChain, developer of a platform to run, improve and govern AI agents, closed on $300 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. CapitalG led the round for the 4-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Nominal, $240M, hardware engineering tools: Nominal, a developer of intelligence tools for hardware engineering, raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners led the round for the Austin-based startup.

7. (tied) Imprint, $130M, fintech: Imprint, a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform for brands, landed $130 million in new funding at a $1.9 billion valuation. Khosla Ventures led the financing for the 6-year-old, New York-based company.

7. (tied) Mavria, $130M, AI infrastructure: Mavria, a startup focused on standardizing how AI infrastructure is developed, built and deployed, launched publicly and said it has raised $130 million in pre-seed and seed funding to date. Its latest round, led by Paradigm, sets a $1 billion valuation for the startup, whose founders formerly worked at the U.S. Department of Energy.

9. (tied) Delix Therapeutics, $100M, biotech: Delix Therapeutics, a startup that says it has “reverse-engineered and optimized psychedelics” to develop treatments for psychiatric and psychological disorders, closed on $100 million in Series C funding. Johnson & Johnson Innovation and SV Health Investors’ Dementia Discovery Fund led the financing for the Bedford, Massachusetts-based company.

9. (tied) Rox, $100M, sales automation: San Francisco-based Rox, developer of an AI revenue agent for enterprise sales, announced a $100 million Series B financing led by General Catalyst and March Capital.

9. (tied) Databento, $100M, financial market data: Databento, a finance data platform, secured $100 million in Series C funding at a $1.1 billion valuation. Fifth Down Capital led the round for the Salt Lake City-based company.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 7-13, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

#5290. ‘AI and Bitcoin Are on One Big Trade Now,’ Says Anthony Pompliano

As Bitcoin’s price continues to fall further, sparking a fresh wave of panic across the broader crypto market, renowned Bitcoin advocate Anthony Pompliano has issued a statement to investors.

In a recent X post published by the pro-Bitcoin advocate on November 13, Pompliano urged investors to remain calm even as Bitcoin revisited $67,000 for the first time since August.

While Pompliano acknowledged the current market weakness, pointing out that Bitcoin was falling to price levels last seen just three months ago, he urged Bitcoin investors to remain calm.

While addressing Bitcoin's price decline, Pompliano related the situation to AI, another fast-growing technology, drawing attention to the growing relationship between the two sectors.

Pompliano considers the ongoing market movements as evidence that both Bitcoin and AI have become part of one major investment trade.

Although he did not explicitly explain how Bitcoin and AI have become one big trade, it appears that Pompliano is raising awareness of how closely investors may now view the two major investment products in the technology and financial markets.

As such, Pompliano is urging investors to remain positive about Bitcoin’s long-term potential, suggesting that the same market forces driving interest in AI could also influence a potential recovery for Bitcoin.

Pompliano’s comment has come as Bitcoin faces renewed selling pressure, retesting its three-month low at around $67,000 after declining over 5% in the last 24 hours.

Bitcoin’s current price movements have raised questions about whether the decline signals a deeper market correction or simply another temporary setback, causing commentators to disagree with Pompliano’s call for confidence.

#5289. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

#5287. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5286. Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.

With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)

The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase is set to suspend trading in 12 crypto trading pairs as part of an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity on the platform. This decision affects two trading pairs involving Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM): ADA/ETH and XLM/BTC.

Coinbase said it regularly monitors the markets on its exchange and, in line with this, trading will be suspended on the named markets on November 25, 2026. In an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, Coinbase will be removing a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

According to an announcement, Coinbase will suspend trading on the following markets on November 25, 2026, at or around 12 PM ET: APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, SNX-GBP.

However, Coinbase Advanced Trade users in eligible regions can still trade these assets in the USD order books.

In light of this, APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP have been moved to limit-only mode on Coinbase Exchange and Coinbase Advanced.

In recent delistings, Coinbase has disabled trading for Balancer (BAL) and Tensor (TNSR), but users will continue to have the ability to withdraw their funds at any time.

The suspension of trading for Stargate Finance (STG) and Vulcan Forged (PYR) has also been postponed to November 20, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Ampleforth Governance Token (FORTH) on November 23, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Trading for Neon EVM (NEON) and Syndicate (SYND) will be suspended on November 16, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET.

Spot trading for Pearl (PEARL) will go live on November 13, 2026. The opening of the PEARL-USD trading pair will begin at or after 9 AM PT, if liquidity conditions are met, in regions where trading is supported.

Perpetual futures trading for GRAM, GRASS, QNT and ZRO will go live on November 13, 2026, at or after 12:00 PM UTC.

The daily trading volume of the NVDA-USDC perpetual contract on the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid has reached a record $2.14 billion, according to CoinGlass. The contract is provided by the Trade.xyz protocol, and only Bitcoin had higher trading volume on Hyperliquid over the same period.

Nvidia futures also surpassed Ethereum, Solana and XRP in trading volume, and the combined volume of Nvidia derivatives across all tracked crypto exchanges reached $9.51 billion, according to CoinGlass.

The latest surge in trading comes amid the resignation of Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia and the only CEO in the history of the company. Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 amid an internal investigation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

On Nasdaq, the price of NVDA went down by as much as 14% during the day, but the stock later recovered most of the loss and closed at $166.19, down 4.34%.

Sharp price moves cost leveraged traders on crypto exchanges $40.86 million, according to CoinGlass. Of that amount, $26.23 million came from the on-chain ticker XYZ:NVDA, and $14.63 million came from the base NVDA contract. The largest single liquidation on Hyperliquid was a $1.54 million long position.

In the base NVDA contract, $8.87 million in long positions and $5.89 million in short positions were liquidated. During the same period, the price of Nvidia futures on crypto exchanges went up by 5.6% to $171.17.

Liquidations in the NVDA contracts were almost twice as large as those in XRP, where traders lost $20.75 million over the same period. The price of XRP went down by 2.5% to $1.0192, and long positions accounted for 94.5% of XRP liquidations, or $19.6 million.

The liquidations came amid a sell-off across major cryptocurrencies. The price of Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 to $69,450.50, down 5.3% over 24 hours, and Ethereum fell 4.1% to $1,958.71.

Over the past 24 hours, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Bitcoin traders lost the most at $919.56 million, followed by Ethereum traders at $297.24 million.

Finally, Nvidia is expected to report its quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.

XRP added almost 20% in open interest on MEXC, which could be a double-edged sword for the price of the asset. Across all exchanges, open interest went up by only 0.86%, reaching $2.25 billion.

XRP is not benefiting directly from an increase in open interest; it could reflect an increase in futures positions.

Futures by themselves are a source of strong volatility and liquidity for assets. Considering the state of the market, XRP's increase in open interest is not unexpected.

Over the past 24 hours, $18.83 million in XRP positions were liquidated, with longs making up 94%.

Futures could be opened by speculative traders who are trying to catch a falling knife. The data, however, suggests that most of the new positions are shorts, as the price went down while open interest went up.

XRP is currently trading at $1.02, down 1.46% over the past 24 hours. The price is approaching the $1 price threshold, and it might be the level where the recovery should finally happen.

Realistically, the closest 'fair' support is the $1 price level, both psychological and technical.

XRP already dipped to $0.9961 earlier today before going back above the threshold. A cluster of long liquidations sits right below that level.

XRP is teetering on the edge of the $1 threshold, which, if broken, essentially enables a rapid decrease.

Funding rates also tilt towards bulls, and there is a good chance we are going to see stabilization and then a recovery. The funding rate sits at 0.0080%, slightly below the 0.01% base, so the tilt is rather small.

In addition, US spot XRP ETFs recorded zero net flows on November 12.

Unfortunately, volume shows an uptick, a direct sign of increasing pressure on the asset. Spot volume went up by 46.7%, with sellers outweighing buyers by $48.2 million.

It is not a guarantee of a bearish market strengthening, but it shows that sellers are there and ready to push the price lower. Whether buyers can defend the $1 level or not is the main test for the asset right now.

#5282. VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’

Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe.

With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital, Atomico and Index Ventures, which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years.

“Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi, a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.”

Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy. In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica, whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co., which develops space transportation.

In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental, which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics, which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub, which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics, which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum, which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute.

Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi.

“Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said.

The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022.

Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026.

The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder of Wise, and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport, both early employees at Skype, as well as Ian Hogarth, co-founder of Songkick, and Khaled Helioui, former CEO of Bigpoint.

The team has two other partners: Carina Namih, co-founder of HelixNano, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty, a former Uber executive.

Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving  bandwidth to work hands-on with founders.

The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and  double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.”

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus, who goes by Shibetoshi Nakamoto on X, responded to an unusual question about his identity, saying, "I am a Shiba Inu."

The markets were shocked by the news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was stepping down as CEO of the chipmaker he co-founded 33 years ago and built into a $4 trillion company that powered the artificial intelligence boom.

The development triggered widespread reactions on social media, with Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus commenting on one of those related posts. Markus’s participation in the discussion, which seemed outside crypto, drew a response from an X user who seemed surprised at his interest in the matter.

"I thought you were a dog," the X user said, obviously referring to his connection with Dogecoin, a dog-themed cryptocurrency launched in December 2013 by Markus himself and Jackson Palmer as a lighthearted alternative to Bitcoin. To this, Markus responded in his characteristic playful manner, saying, "I am a Shiba Inu."

In another X reply, the Dogecoin cofounder reiterated that "Billy is a Shiba Inu with glasses."

Markus’s response is a tribute to Dogecoin’s lasting association with its early internet meme roots, with the Shiba Inu dog integral to the cryptocurrency’s identity. The Dogecoin cofounder's response also serves as a reminder of the playful personality that helped distinguish Dogecoin from other digital assets during its early years.

The markets slumped early Friday as traders priced in a Fed rate increase next month, strengthening the dollar, raising bond yields and making riskier assets less attractive.

Thursday's resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also impacted the crypto market and sent shares of the AI chip maker, the world’s second-largest company by market cap, tumbling 4%. At the time of writing, Dogecoin was down 0.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.0659 and down 7% weekly.

Leveraged traders took the brunt, as liquidations surged 150% to $1.4 billion, with longs making up the majority of the wipeout at $1.16 billion while shorts came in at $245 million.

#5280. In The AI Era, Keep Hiring New College Grads — And Make Them Managers From Day One

A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI.

Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?”

The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children?

College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic, a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening.

What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that.

Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams.

The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution.

The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong.

Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management.

These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives, naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers.

It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win.

I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management.

The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner.

When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage.

This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face.

In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July.

This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management.

As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled:

“When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?”

Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot’s store management program and General Electric’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done.

Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds.

First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed.

Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care.

Third, the service academies build high-pressure situations into their leadership laboratory. While most companies are not placing their first-line managers in life or death situations, the ability to lead in high stakes situations, for instance to take personal responsibility for an AI agent swarm you launched which is now “going rogue,” requires composure and decisiveness under stress and pressure.

If a 22-year-old ensign can manage 25 sailors on a Yokosuka destroyer, albeit with support from senior officers and enlisted, our 22-year-old college graduate can certainly be trained to manage 25 super-intelligent agents. The moment for practicing the craft of management will shift from 32 years old to 22 years old, across the businesses of knowledge work.

In short: We need to bring back the “managing analyst.” We need to recognize that AI agents behave like knowledge workers and therefore need to be managed. We should reset the culture in knowledge work industries that management is a valued skill, beginning at the start of one’s career and not midcareer.

These entry-level workers are smart, motivated, learn quickly and work hard. There is a huge unmet need for the craft of management in corralling this new generation of AI agents. We have the proof points across nearly 200 years from our service academies that these skills can be taught to the young, and the young can deliver them with distinction. The future for college graduates is a redefinition of their jobs away from being individual-contributor knowledge workers and toward being effective managers and leaders from the very beginning of their careers.

Bob Morse co-founded Strattam Capital in 2014 and is managing partner. He has served on numerous private and public technology company boards, and currently is a director of CloudHesive, Contegix, Daxtra Technologies, Green Security, Resource Navigation and Trax Group. Previously, he was a partner and member of the investment committee at Oak Hill Capital Partners. He also worked at GCC Investments and Morgan Stanley. Morse serves on the board of directors of Austin PBS and as member of the advisory board for the HMTF Center for Private Equity Finance at The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business. He attended Princeton University, graduating summa cum laude with a BSE, and Stanford Graduate School of Business, where he earned his MBA and was an Arjay Miller Scholar. Morse lives in Austin.

Michael Quoia is co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership, which assesses and develops leaders and teams. A 25-year leadership advisory veteran with partner-level roles at Heidrick & Struggles and Russell Reynolds Associates, he began his career as a U.S. Navy  surface warfare officer. He is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy and holds an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business.

#5278. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

#5277. Japanese Giant Rakuten Joins Institutional XRP ETF Holders

Japanese tech and fintech conglomerate Rakuten Group is among the institutional holders of a U.S. spot XRP ETF, according to the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Rakuten also holds funds tracking Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana, and these positions were worth roughly $6.42 million combined at the end of the quarter on Sept. 30, 2026.

The filing shows that Rakuten held 6,690 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF worth $111,255. At press time, the price of XRP stands at $1.03, and the shares of the Bitwise fund trade at $11.51, according to SoSoValue, so the XRP ETF stake of Rakuten is now worth about $77,000.

Rakuten is not the only institutional investor in the new XRP funds, and Raymond James Financial has also disclosed positions in spot XRP ETFs, according to SEC filings.

The largest position of Rakuten is in BlackRock's spot Bitcoin fund, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, and Rakuten held $5,893,593 worth of its shares at the end of the third quarter. Besides, Rakuten owns $263,632 of the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF and $150,728 of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF.

U.S. rules require any institutional manager holding more than $100 million in U.S. exchange-listed securities to disclose its portfolio every quarter, no matter where it's based. Rakuten Group holds about $1.4 billion in U.S. equities, and most of that amount is in shares of satellite operator AST SpaceMobile. In this context, the crypto ETF positions account for less than 0.5% of the U.S. portfolio of Rakuten.

Rakuten is one of the largest tech companies in Japan. The market capitalization of Rakuten stands at about ¥1.4 trillion ($9 billion), and the annual revenue of the company is more than ¥2.5 trillion ($16 billion).

The Rakuten ecosystem spans more than 70 services, from the Rakuten Ichiba marketplace and carrier Rakuten Mobile to banks and brokerages. According to Rakuten, these services have more than 100 million users in Japan and more than 2.1 billion users worldwide.

The latest filing comes amid outflows from spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds lost $10.42 million on Nov. 9 and another $7.62 million on Nov. 10, and there were no flows on Nov. 11 and Nov. 12. On Oct. 28, the total net assets of the funds stood at $1.51 billion.

Still, the cumulative net inflow of spot XRP ETFs stands at $1.79 billion, and the total net assets of the funds are $1.16 billion, or 1.77% of the market cap of XRP. Finally, the Bitwise XRP ETF is the largest of the five spot XRP funds, and its net assets stand at $420.29 million, according to SoSoValue.

#5276. Binance Pays Microsoft and Applied Materials Dividends on Tokenized Stocks: How Much Holders Get

Binance said on Monday, November 16, that it will pass the next Microsoft and Applied Materials cash dividends to holders of its tokenized stocks, MSFTB and AMATB. It will snapshot balances on Thursday, November 19, the same day both stocks go ex-dividend.

Tokenized stocks are crypto tokens that track a real share, held by a custodian, and trade around the clock. Binance’s versions, called bStocks, do not pay the dividend in cash. Instead, the net amount is reinvested, and each holder’s token balance grows slightly.

We compared both tokens with the real shares since late August. During market hours, they tracked closely. Over weekends, their price called Monday’s opening move only half the time.

Here is what holders get, and what the token prices tell traders this week.

Both companies declared their payouts in September. Microsoft will pay $0.98 a share, up from $0.91. Applied Materials, a maker of chipmaking equipment, will pay $0.53 a share. Both go to shareholders of record on November 19 and are paid on December 10.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

Binance does not state the tax rate. The standard U.S. rate on dividends paid to foreign holders without a tax treaty is 30%. At that rate, we worked out what holders get:

A dividend only matters if the token tracks the stock. So we compared both tokens with the real shares, using Binance hourly candles and Nasdaq prices since late August.

During market hours, the match is close. At the Nasdaq close, the tokens sat at a median 0.06% from the official closing price across 58 sessions. The widest gap was 0.28%.

Weekends are different. The tokens keep trading while Wall Street is shut, so we checked whether their weekend price predicted Monday’s opening move.

Thin trading in tokenized stocks explains part of it. MSFTB traded about $183,000 in the past 24 hours on Binance, and AMATB about $114,000. This weekend, AMATB stood 1.8% below Friday’s $370.50 close on Sunday night, while MSFTB was down 0.2%. On our numbers, those weekend quotes said little about where the stocks would open.

On the 4-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, MSFTB trades at $527.61 on Binance. It sits just above its 50-period exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $526.02, and its 200-period EMA at $526.95. With both averages flat and close together, the trend is neutral.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

For holders of tokenized stocks, the dividend adds about a tenth of a percent to their balance this quarter. The bigger lesson is in timing: on weekdays, the tokens follow the stock, but weekend prices are a weak guide to Monday.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Stellar (XLM), the blockchain co-founded by Jed McCaleb, has become the leader in daily market cap growth for tokenized real-world asset (RWA) funds, according to Token Terminal data published by the RWA Foundation. Over the 24 hours to Nov. 13, the market cap of tokenized funds on Stellar went up by $44.9 million, and the network surpassed both Ethereum and Solana.

Over the same period, the market cap of tokenized funds on Solana, Ethereum and zkSync Era increased by $29 million, $10.8 million and $3.5 million, respectively.

Stellar is currently the second-largest blockchain for tokenized funds after Ethereum, according to Token Terminal. Over the past year, the RWA market on Stellar has grown roughly sixfold and reached $4.67 billion, according to rwa.xyz. At press time, the price of XLM stands at $0.1476.

According to the Stellar Development Foundation, Stellar was designed with the requirements of banks and transfer agents in mind. In this context, the compliance tools are built into the base layer of the network, and an issuer can vet investors through trustlines, freeze accounts and claw back assets.

Transactions on Stellar settle in 3 to 5 seconds, and the fees on the network are measured in fractions of a cent. Besides, users can move funds to and from fiat currencies through local providers, which are called anchors on Stellar.

Franklin Templeton's BENJI money market fund has run on Stellar since 2021, and it was the first U.S. mutual fund on a public blockchain.

Today, Spiko, Ondo and WisdomTree are also building their own funds and tokenized U.S. Treasuries on Stellar. Spiko offers euro funds managed by Amundi, and Ondo has launched its USDY token on the network.

In May 2026, DTCC and the Stellar Development Foundation announced that the Depository Trust Company (DTC) will tokenize the assets it holds in custody on Stellar. According to DTCC, DTC-tokenized assets are expected to become available on the network in the first half of 2027.

On Nov. 12, DTCC also announced that it will connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.
