#5166. 178 Websites Infected in Major Optimizely Hack: Crypto Wallets Targeted, but Bitcoin Barely Reacted

Optimizely attack infects 178 websites, steals crypto and card data, and exposes users to wallet-address swaps and iPhone exploits.

An Optimizely attack on Monday, November 16, planted crypto-stealing code on the websites of 178 organizations, including Ledger, HSBC, Zoom, the BBC and CNN. The malicious script swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card numbers, and tried to break into iPhones for about 19 hours before it was cleaned up.

BREAKING: A cyberattack hit 178 major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, BBC, Fox News, HSBC, Ledger, Equifax, Salesforce, IKEA and Air France-KLM, by loading malware on the Optimizely Web platform, exposing visitors to scripts built to steal payment data and exploit iOS…

— The Hormuz Letter (@HormuzLetter) November 17, 2026

Optimizely is a tool companies use to test different versions of their web pages. An attacker slipped code into the scripts it serves, so every site that loaded them ran the malware.

We traced the attacker’s Bitcoin wallet. It received five payments worth about $5,500, and one victim alone sent nearly 90% of it. Bitcoin barely moved while the attack ran.

So what happened, and what is the real impact of hacks like this one?

Security researcher Scott Helme of Report URI found the code and published a full breakdown. The attacker wrote it into a settings field in customers’ Optimizely projects, so it was served from Optimizely’s own servers and looked legitimate.

Optimizely said it “secured affected user accounts and added protections against further unauthorized code delivery.” Report URI found no sign that Ledger hardware wallets themselves were breached. The danger was on the website, where a copied address could be swapped before a user pasted it.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Security Analyst Recommends Best Anonymous Crypto Wallets

Report URI listed the attacker’s wallets. We checked the Bitcoin one on mempool.space, the public Bitcoin block explorer.

The Optimizely attack’s impact was tiny, and the market ignored it. Bitcoin is near $64,300 after its weekend low of $62,006, and that slide came from wider selling, not this attack.

EXPLORE: Crypto Hack Losses Hit $8.74 Billion in 2026, More Than Triple 2025: How Did Bitcoin and Ether React?

The money stolen in the Optimizely attack is small, but the method is the year’s most damaging one. We sorted DefiLlama’s 2026 hack list by attack type. Attacks on websites and infrastructure, rather than on smart contracts, are now the costliest category:

These attacks hit users where no wallet setting can protect them. The fix is on the user’s side: check the address on the hardware wallet’s screen before signing, send a small test transfer first, and keep phones updated.

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $64,326. It sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $76,208, and its 200-day EMA at $75,864.

The Optimizely attack did not move Bitcoin, and the attacker walked away with about $7,000. Its real cost is trust: when a hardware-wallet maker’s own website can serve malware for hours, checking every address on the device is no longer optional.

#5165. Figment to Support Staking Through BNY’s Digital Asset Custody Platform

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

BNY’s digital asset custody business is adding another route into staking through a collaboration with Figment. The development addresses a practical institutional problem: earning protocol rewards while keeping assets within an established custody and reporting relationship.

In its November 12 announcement, Figment said its validators would support BNY’s staking offering for eligible clients. The release names asset managers, ETF issuers, corporations and wealth managers among the potential users, without providing a launch date or a universal list of eligible accounts.

The arrangement combines BNY’s custody and servicing framework with Figment’s infrastructure for participating in blockchain validation. That allows the two providers to supply different parts of one client workflow.

Holding an asset safely and using it in a protocol are related responsibilities, but they require different operations. Custody focuses on control, safekeeping and administration. Validator infrastructure performs the continuing network duties that can generate staking rewards.

For a large investment firm, integration can reduce the number of separate processes its staff must coordinate. Reconciliation, permissions and reporting still need to work across the whole arrangement, however. A convenient interface does not make those responsibilities disappear; it gives the providers a defined place to organize them.

BNY had already outlined a staking collaboration with Galaxy in an August 4 announcement. That release described an integrated institutional service and said the offering and related infrastructure enhancements were subject to regulatory review.

The Figment announcement therefore should not be framed as BNY discovering staking for the first time. It is another development in the infrastructure supporting a previously stated direction.

NewsBTC’s coverage of BNY’s European custody expansion under MiCA provides a second part of that history. Geographic permissions, supported assets and individual client eligibility remain specific to the relevant service and entity.

Ethereum’s staking documentation explains that validators receive rewards for performing network duties. Downtime can lead to missed rewards and penalties, while certain forms of misconduct can cause slashing. Using a provider adds operational and counterparty considerations to that protocol exposure.

The economic distinction is straightforward. A holder can accumulate more units of an asset while the value of the position falls in dollars. Staking income and market-price performance are different components of the final result.

NewsBTC examined that distinction in its report on Sygnum’s ETH-denominated investment fund. That fund includes separate trading strategies, so its target should not be imported into the BNY service as though it were a quoted staking rate.

The potential benefit is an easier operational route for institutions that already hold supported digital assets with a custodian. That could matter to firms whose investment policy allows staking but whose internal processes make managing validators directly impractical.

Actual adoption would need to be judged through live availability, assets staked, service performance and the terms clients receive. Fees, exit arrangements, reporting quality and responsibility for operational losses would all affect the proposition, even if the underlying protocol reward were identical.

The announcement does not disclose those commercial details or a guaranteed level of participation. It establishes the collaboration and the intended access model. Delivering a service that institutions can use consistently, within their own mandates and liquidity needs, is the next practical test.

#5163. SOL Eyes New Bullish Era as Solana Ditches ‘Beta’ Label After Six Years and Embraces Protocol Version 1.0

Solana has officially turned a major page in its history, dropping the long-standing ‘beta’ tag after more than six years and adopting protocol version 1.0. The milestone marks a significant step in the network’s evolution as it moves beyond its experimental phase, with ongoing efforts to improve transaction speed, finality, and overall performance. The development could also strengthen Solana’s appeal to developers and institutional players, raising fresh questions about whether SOL is poised for a new bullish chapter.

Solana has officially retired its six-year-old “mainnet beta” designation, with the network’s foundation saying the rebranding highlights the significant strides made since the blockchain first launched in March 2020.

“Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience,” the Solana foundation wrote in a Monday statement. “That progress continues with this simplification of nomenclature.”

The foundation emphasized that Solana has operated as a fully live network since its launch, arguing that retaining the beta designation had become outdated. It noted that the label, traditionally associated with technology still in its early testing stages, no longer accurately represented a blockchain already processing transactions and hosting active applications.

According to the Solana Foundation, the reclassification requires no action from users. Existing SOL holdings, account balances, and transaction histories will remain unchanged despite the protocol’s transition to version 1.0.

The foundation also advised developers and validator operators to stick to the specific instructions accompanying software releases, stressing that the new protocol designation does not mean all network upgrades or improvements become active automatically.

Solana’s move to protocol version 1.0 comes as the network continues pursuing major infrastructure improvements, with Alpenglow and Firedancer among its most closely watched developments. Both initiatives aim to strengthen Solana’s performance, reliability, and ability to support growing on-chain activity.

The first major milestone is Alpenglow, Solana’s new consensus protocol, which went live on mainnet on October 21. The upgrade targets transaction finality of approximately 150 milliseconds, a significant improvement from the previous 12.8-second timeframe. Transaction finality refers to the moment a blockchain permanently confirms a transaction, meaning it is considered settled and cannot be reversed under normal network conditions. Faster finality could make Solana more attractive for payments, decentralized finance, and institutional applications that require near-instant transaction settlement.

Meanwhile, Firedancer brings another important improvement through an independently developed validator client built by Jump Crypto. It provides an alternative to Solana’s existing Agave client, reducing the network’s dependence on a single software implementation. This client diversity could strengthen network resilience by limiting the risk that a bug affecting one implementation disrupts the entire blockchain.

The foundation added that the rebranding establishes a unified system for tracking Solana’s updates, allowing developers, validators, and infrastructure providers to identify protocol changes consistently, regardless of the software client they use.

#5161. JPMorgan and MIT Map More Than 150 Requirements for Institutional Blockchains

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

JPMorgan’s Kinexys and the MIT Digital Currency Initiative have put a detailed question to public-blockchain developers: how much of what banks need can a network accommodate while retaining the qualities that made it attractive? A November 13 discussion paper identifies more than 150 institutional requirements and invites the industry to work through the tensions.

The Kinexys announcement highlights sanctions compliance, accountable governance, client confidentiality and interoperability. The paper is a starting point for discussion, with a further whitepaper intended to reflect responses. It does not certify a particular chain as suitable for regulated finance.

The underlying trade-off is easy to see. A bank may value infrastructure that no competitor controls, yet still need someone to answer for an outage or implement a legally required restriction. Giving one operator extensive powers could make that responsibility clearer while changing the network’s neutrality. The right arrangement may vary between a payment token, a trading venue and an asset register.

An earlier MIT and Kinexys report published in June examined transaction front-running, omitted transactions, unsolicited tokens and sanctions exposure through network fees. Its layered framework separates changes an institution can make inside an application from changes requiring cooperation at protocol, governance or regulatory level.

That distinction helps explain why a polished banking interface cannot settle every underlying question. A customer-facing application might reject an instruction, but it cannot necessarily stop another blockchain participant from sending a token to the bank’s address. Likewise, internal approval controls do not by themselves determine how validators order transactions.

These are concrete operating questions for firms already experimenting with public networks. NewsBTC’s coverage of JPM Coin on Ethereum illustrates how restricted institutional participation can coexist with public-chain infrastructure.

The research partners have also examined payment-token standards, including how transaction information and administrative recovery controls can be represented. That work proposes more targeted, composable capabilities instead of assuming one broad token standard will satisfy every banking use case.

Consider a transfer that is technically valid but sent to an unintended eligible recipient. The business needs a process for investigating the error and deciding whether remediation is possible. A token with administrative controls may offer options, but those controls create their own questions about authority, access and misuse. Making a function available in code is only part of deciding who may invoke it.

Settlement design adds another layer. As NewsBTC’s examination of Solana’s delivery-versus-payment tool shows, coordinating the asset and payment legs addresses a specific transaction problem. It does not settle every question about custody, eligibility or governance around that transaction.

A long requirements list will be valuable if it helps participants identify which demands are essential, which belong at a different layer and which cannot coexist without compromise. Simply adding every requested control could produce a costly system whose advantages over existing infrastructure are difficult to explain.

There is also a coordination problem. A bank can approve its own software release, but a shared network may depend on participants with different incentives and upgrade schedules. Institutions therefore need to assess how changes are agreed, how dissent is handled and what continuity means when a network evolves.

The discussion paper makes those decisions explicit. Its next contribution will depend on whether developers, institutions and policymakers can turn broad requirements into practical arrangements with identifiable responsibility. That is a more demanding test of adoption than announcing another token on an existing chain.

Solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation said.

Solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status."

The Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

According to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once."

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

#5157. SBI and Cambodia Plan a Yen Stablecoin Trial Behind Everyday Remittances

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

SBI Holdings and the National Bank of Cambodia plan to test a yen stablecoin for transfers between Japan and Cambodia. The proposed design puts JPYSC between financial institutions, leaving customers with a familiar way to send and receive money. That makes this a test of payment infrastructure behind the scenes, rather than a proposal that remittance users manage a new crypto wallet themselves.

SBI’s November 13 announcement describes a closed-loop proof of concept examining regulation, systems and commercial viability. The group will provide banking, remittance and token infrastructure, while Cambodia’s central bank supplies regulatory guidance and reviews the work. The proposal is intended to complement the country’s Bakong payment system.

The customer-facing distinction is significant. A sender usually wants to know the fee, exchange rate and amount the recipient can use. If the institutions change their settlement method without changing that experience, the technology succeeds only if it improves the complete payment journey.

A quicker transfer between two providers could still leave a recipient waiting if local payout or currency conversion is unavailable. The trial therefore needs to evaluate both the digital settlement leg and its connection to ordinary balances.

The June launch announcement identifies SBI Shinsei Trust Bank as JPYSC’s issuer and SBI VC Trade as its distributor. Initial use was limited to accounts at SBI VC Trade, with external-wallet transfers unavailable at that stage. That historical access condition should not be mistaken for proof that every proposed cross-border use is already operational.

The trust-based structure, discussed in NewsBTC’s earlier JPYSC coverage, distinguishes the token from a floating-price cryptocurrency. Its intended reference is the yen, while the rights and operational route depend on the issuer and service terms. A customer paying a Cambodian expense still has a currency-conversion question even if the intermediate settlement asset maintains its yen value.

NewsBTC has covered other proposed uses, including linking JPYSC with tokenized investment funds. A common settlement asset can serve different workflows, but each connection needs its own implementation and permissions.

SBI also disclosed a distinct agreement to test tokenized Cambodian government bonds. That experiment is planned on Canton Network, with the National Bank of Cambodia managing bondholder information. The announcement leaves service details and timing to further discussion.

The two projects should not be combined into a claim that investors can buy Cambodian bonds with JPYSC. Neither release establishes such a transaction or a technical bridge between Canton and Bakong. One examines remittance settlement; the other examines how a government-bond holding and transfer can be represented.

Tokenizing a bond changes its representation and transfer process; it does not remove the issuer’s repayment obligation or the investor’s need to understand it. A remittance settlement token performs a different task. The legal claims behind those assets remain central even if both use blockchain technology.

The remittance announcement schedules interim findings and a demonstration for the Black Swan Summit on November 15–16. It does not establish a commercial launch date, a customer tariff or achieved savings. Those remain questions for evidence from the work and any subsequent service announcement.

For a meaningful comparison, the partners would need to consider the amount delivered after all fees and conversion, the time until it becomes usable and the process when a payment cannot complete. A low blockchain transaction fee alone cannot describe those outcomes.

The proposed trial gives yen stablecoins a specific task: improve the settlement arrangement behind a defined payment corridor. Its value will depend on whether institutions can turn that arrangement into a dependable service for people and businesses moving money between the two countries.

The advertised 1.1 million USDT in prizes covers several types of rewards, rather than direct cash payouts alone. These include fee cashback, trading-related rewards and prizes tied to competition results and trading volumes.

#5154. Kenya Directs Crypto Providers to Apply for VASP Licences

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Kenya’s central bank and capital-markets regulator have told businesses providing virtual-asset services to apply for licences under the country’s VASP framework. Their November 13 notice brings attention to the practical application process: firms now have to explain what they do, who controls them and how customer transactions will work.

The joint CBK and CMA notice says the implementing regulations were gazetted on July 22, 2026. The underlying Act dates to 2025. November’s development is therefore a regulatory direction about putting the framework into operation, rather than a law created this week.

Providers are assigned to the Central Bank of Kenya or the Capital Markets Authority according to their services. That structure makes the business model central to the application. Calling an app a wallet or an exchange is not enough to explain whether it also processes payments, holds assets or issues a token.

The distinction has a regional parallel in Nigeria’s separate stablecoin licensing rules. African markets are developing their own frameworks, with different activities and responsible agencies. An operator cannot treat a licence in one country as a general permission to serve the continent.

The CBK’s licensing checklist covers stablecoin issuers, virtual-asset payment processors and wallet providers. Preliminary submissions include a business-model presentation, three-year projections, an organisational structure, customer journeys and fund flows. Applicants must disclose cross-border operations and their regulatory status elsewhere.

Those requests reach beyond whether a platform’s software works. A regulator examining a customer journey wants to understand where funds enter, which entity controls them and what the user receives at each step. A company relying on several overseas partners would need to describe those handoffs clearly.

For a prospective customer or banking partner, the same map can reveal practical dependencies. If a wallet provider relies on a separate issuer for redemption, a successful token transfer is not the same as receipt of spendable local currency. Each stage has an accountable party, even when the interface presents one seamless service.

The implementing regulations set out application and licensing requirements. The published checklist then turns that framework into a staged process, covering preliminary engagement, names and formal company documentation. It specifies a non-refundable application fee of 100,000 Kenyan shillings for each activity sought.

The fee should not be confused with the total resources needed to operate. Preparing reliable records, managing access to customer assets and maintaining the people and systems behind a service can be much more consequential than submitting an application. A firm offering several activities also has to ensure that its documentation describes how they interact.

Ghana’s crypto sandbox programme offers another regional example of regulators moving from broad policy statements to defined business assessments. Kenya’s notice concerns its own licensing process, so the conditions of that separate sandbox do not transfer across borders.

The regulators say they will publish lists of licensed providers. The notice itself names no approved firm and gives no application deadline. A company announcing that it has applied should therefore be described as an applicant until the responsible authority confirms a licence.

That distinction gives customers a useful way to evaluate future announcements. They can compare the legal entity and permitted activity against the official record, rather than rely solely on a platform’s brand or a claim that it is regulated somewhere.

The commercial consequences will emerge as applications are assessed. Clearer responsibilities may help credible businesses build relationships, while compliance costs could change which services smaller operators can sustain. Kenya has made the application route more concrete; actual authorisations will show how the market develops under it.

Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, spent $228.1 million buying back its STRC preferred stock between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, according to the company's new filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Over the same period, Strategy bought 485 BTC for $33.4 million, so the company spent almost seven times more on STRC than on Bitcoin.

"Strategy has acquired 485 BTC and repurchased $228M of STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets," Michael Saylor wrote on X.

The filing shows that Strategy sold 2.09 million shares of its Class A common stock and raised $244.7 million. The company used $206.3 million of that amount for STRC buybacks and added another $21.8 million from interest earned on its dollar reserves.

The 485 BTC were bought at an average price of $68,887 per coin. The remaining $5 million from the share sales stayed on the books as free cash.

STRC, also known as Stretch, is a perpetual preferred stock with a variable monthly dividend, and Strategy launched it in July 2025.

When the price of Bitcoin slipped below $65,000, STRC fell to $99.08. Strategy aims to keep STRC close to its $100 par value, and the company has another $332.2 million set aside for buybacks. The board of Strategy also approved a December STRC dividend at an annual rate of 12%, or $1.00 per share.

"USD Duration is 3.4 yrs and STRC's BTC Credit tightened to 67 bps (-3 bps), assuming 10% BTC ARR, 40% BTC Vol, and a BTC price of $68,800," Saylor added.

As of Nov. 15, Strategy held 850,849 BTC, bought for a total of $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. On Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $63,941, and Strategy's holdings are worth around $54.4 billion.

The unrealized loss of the company on its Bitcoin holdings stands at around $9.8 billion. On Sunday, when the price of Bitcoin fell to $62,029 on Bitfinex, the loss was above $11 billion.

Strategy also holds $4.9 billion in dollar assets, and $4.75 billion of that amount is in its dedicated USD reserve.

#5151. Circle Expands Disparte and Walia Roles as Stablecoin Operations Scale

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Circle is expanding the responsibilities of two senior executives as its stablecoin business faces a more demanding mix of regulation and institutional operations. Dante Disparte becomes vice chairman for strategy and global affairs, while compliance and risk chief Mandeep Walia also takes on the chief operating officer role. The November 13 announcement puts governance design alongside the company’s growth ambitions.

That assurance is relevant because the functions can face competing pressures. An operations team wants customers onboarded and payments completed efficiently. A control function may need to delay an activity, investigate a concern or challenge a proposed product. Combining senior responsibilities can improve coordination, but effective escalation still requires a route for concerns to reach decision-makers.

The announcement does not identify a regulatory failure or say that the appointments respond to one. Its significance is the organisation Circle is choosing for the next stage of its business.

Circle’s transparency disclosures describe reserves held separately from operating funds, weekly information on USDC holdings and issuance flows, and monthly third-party assurance. Those reporting practices address the backing of the token. They are one part of the wider service customers depend on.

A business receiving a stablecoin payment also needs reliable account access, reconciliation and support when a transfer is delayed or disputed. Even a fully funded reserve does not automatically tell a customer whether a particular intermediary can process its request at a particular time.

That is why the organisational link between payments and risk management deserves attention. A growing network can produce more varied customer journeys, counterparties and exceptions. The challenge is to handle that variety without losing a consistent view of balances, permissions and unresolved issues.

The European Banking Authority’s USDC decision provides one example of the regulatory environment. From November 12, the EBA took responsibility for specified prudential matters, while France’s ACPR retained other oversight functions. NewsBTC covered that supervisory change separately.

For an issuer operating across jurisdictions, this kind of division makes clear ownership of information important. Different supervisors may need different evidence about reserves, governance or recovery arrangements. An internal team has to know which legal entity, process and responsible officer each request concerns.

Disparte’s strategy and global-affairs role sits against that backdrop. Regulatory engagement can help explain a company’s business model and planned services, but an executive appointment does not itself create permission to operate in a new market. The relevant licences and conditions still govern each activity.

Circle’s earlier collaboration with ACI Worldwide explores placing USDC settlement within existing payment operations in Colombia. As NewsBTC’s report on that project explained, the work concerns integration with established systems rather than an automatic switch of all payments to stablecoins.

That type of customer may care as much about exception handling and consistent records as about blockchain speed. A bank assessing a new settlement option needs to understand how it fits its treasury controls, how incidents are communicated and who resolves a mismatch between two systems.

The new roles therefore deserve to be judged through the quality of Circle’s operations and oversight as those relationships develop. Titles describe who is accountable at the top; dependable service and independent challenge show whether the arrangement works in practice.

#5149. US and Canada Announce Massive Crypto Fraud Crackdown

Authorities in the United States and Canada have announced a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) announced on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," said Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

#5148. stUSDT Begins Wind-Down as JustLend Plans to Remove Its Wrapped Token Market

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

The stUSDT protocol is winding down, turning attention from the yield its token offered to the process through which holders can recover the underlying USDT. The affected product is a receipt token linked to deposits and off-chain investment activity.

The team’s redemption announcement ended reward accrual on November 14. JustLend subsequently outlined how it plans to remove the wrapped version, wstUSDT, from its lending markets. Together, the notices show why closing a financial product can involve more than switching off its website.

The team says its web redemption service will remain available until May 14, 2027, at 23:59 UTC. Later requests are to be handled through customer support in monthly batches through August 2027. It says the underlying assets remain fully backed.

That is the issuer’s statement about backing and its proposed process. Successful execution will depend on holders being able to complete redemptions and on the assets being available when required. The notice does not explain the commercial reason for the closure.

A long application window also should not be confused with immediate liquidity for every position. Tokens held inside another protocol may first be subject to that platform’s withdrawal, collateral or debt arrangements. The route depends on where the holder’s claim currently sits.

In its November 14 notice, JustLend described a first phase that would disable new supply and borrowing in the wstUSDT market. Existing positions would remain manageable during the transition, with further parameter changes to follow.

The accompanying governance proposal anticipates further proposals around late November covering collateral and reserve factors. These are planned steps, and the announcement should not be read as proof that every change has already been executed.

For a lending market, that sequencing matters. Preventing new exposure stops the position from growing while giving existing participants time to unwind. Later changes to collateral treatment can alter borrowing capacity, making the details of subsequent governance decisions financially relevant.

A 2024 ChainSecurity assessment describes stUSDT as a custodial system in which deposits support off-chain investments. Its wrapped token keeps balances non-rebasing, which helps compatibility with other contracts. The report explicitly excludes off-chain components from its review.

That historical description helps explain the structure; it cannot establish today’s reserves. Reviewing software answers questions about how contracts behave within a defined scope. Establishing that the corresponding investment assets exist and can be realized requires additional evidence.

NewsBTC covered questions about stUSDT’s use in exchange reserves in 2023. That earlier debate provides context for the product’s history, without establishing a reason for the current wind-down.

The expansion of tokenized finance has produced many different sources of return, including the reinsurance-linked products NewsBTC recently examined. Their assets and risks differ, but each needs a clear account of how a holder exits.

For stUSDT, the useful evidence now will be completed redemptions, clear handling of wrapped balances and precise notices from platforms that previously accepted the token. Holders with outstanding borrowing obligations also need the lending-market process to remain understandable throughout the transition.

The shutdown announcement supplies a timetable. The stronger test is whether the protocol and its integrations can follow that timetable while keeping the connection between token balances, underlying claims and actual payments clear.

#5146. Is The $30B XRP Burn Offer Acceptable For Ripple?

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Is The $30B XRP Burn Offer Acceptable For Ripple?

A courageous plan to burn more than half of the remaining XRP supply lands on Ripple’s table.

Lawyer and longtime XRP observer Bill Morgan reacted to a fresh call for Ripple to destroy its entire escrow by stating the obvious: “Imagine asking a company to destroy an asset valued at $30 billion, believe they would ever do it, and expect to be viewed as sane.”

The demand in question came from an open letter urging Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse to burn the full remaining escrow, currently about 31.1 billion XRP, by the first quarter of 2027. At recent prices near $0.95, that amount is worth roughly $30 billion.

Ripple locked 55 billion XRP into on-ledger escrow contracts in December, 2017 specifically to make supply more predictable.

Each month, up to 1 billion XRP becomes available; historically, the company has re-locked the majority into new smart contracts further down the line and retained a smaller net amount for operational use.

It would make more sense for XRPL validators to vote on any major supply change, because the XRP Ledger is decentralized. Ripple runs only a small share of the default Unique Node List (roughly 1 of ~35, or low single-digit percent).Protocol amendments require ~80% of trusted… https://t.co/Ib7cTsQHUx

The escrow balance has already declined from 55 billion to roughly 31.1 billion as a result of this process.

Destroying the remaining escrow would mean permanently removing an asset that sits on Ripple’s balance sheet and that the company has repeatedly said is intended for controlled distribution, partnerships, and ecosystem growth.

No public company has ever willingly incinerated tens of billions of dollars in assets simply because a segment of token holders asked for it.

Morgan has addressed similar proposals before. He has pointed out that large burns by other projects, including Stellar’s well-known reduction of its XLM supply, did not produce lasting price strength or prevent later declines.

The recurring demand to burn the XRP escrow, in his view, often functions more as a signal that the requester doubts the asset’s underlying value than as a coherent supply-side strategy.

Critics of the XRP escrow schedule frequently treat every monthly unlock as an automatic dump that suppresses price.

In practice, the majority of each release is returned to escrow, and XRP’s price has continued to move largely in line with broader crypto market conditions rather than in lockstep with the XRP escrow schedule.

The supply was never meant to last forever. At the current net release rate of roughly 300 million XRP per month, the locked supply continues to decline gradually.

Imagine asking a company to destroy an asset valued at $30 billion, believe they would ever do it, and expect to be viewed as sane https://t.co/sft8TRMV80

Morgan the lawyer has also noted in earlier posts that the escrow has already fallen from 55 billion in late 2017 to the low-to-mid 30s of billions today.

That full distribution under the original monthly cap would have emptied it years ago had Ripple not retained the flexibility to re-lock unused amounts.

#5145. Binance Says Withdrawals Reopened on 87 Networks as Recovery Moves Toward Full Access

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Binance’s recovery has reached another practical milestone: the exchange says it reopened withdrawals across 87 networks during the week covered by its November 14 update. For customers waiting to move assets, that is more immediately useful than a general assurance about reserves.

The company notice targets reopening the remaining networks and assets by the end of the following week. It is a target for the restoration programme, rather than confirmation that every supported route is already operating.

The update names networks including Cardano, Avalanche, Stellar, Litecoin and NEAR. Binance asks customers to confirm the particular asset and network in its withdrawal interface, and warns that the rollout can involve processing delays.

The distinction between an asset and a network is operationally important. A token can be supported on more than one blockchain, while a customer’s receiving service may accept only a particular version. A broad announcement therefore cannot replace confirmation of the actual route at the time of transfer.

This extends the phased process described in NewsBTC’s report on the November 3 restart. The latest notice adds a larger disclosed set of restored networks and a target for the remaining work.

In a separate coverage announcement, Binance said it had completed replacement of affected assets after committing more than $6.34 billion of company resources. It described funding from SAFU, part of its futures insurance fund and its treasury.

The same disclosure said a November 12 reserve snapshot covered 198 tokens and that Binance intended to replenish SAFU to about $1 billion. These are company statements about funding and backing, with their own verification requirements.

They answer a different question from whether a customer can withdraw immediately. Restoring a balance, rebuilding an emergency reserve and enabling reliable transfers can progress at different speeds. Combining them into a single recovery percentage would hide the remaining operational work.

Binance’s proof-of-reserves explanation describes cryptographic checks that let customers confirm inclusion of their balances in a liabilities snapshot. Its system uses Merkle trees and zero-knowledge proofs to assess the relationship between included account data and the reported total.

That can provide useful evidence about the balances covered by a particular assessment. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that every security weakness has been removed or that every withdrawal request will process successfully.

NewsBTC recently examined the scope and limits of Bybit’s reserve reporting. The general lesson applies here too: readers need to know the date, assets and liabilities covered before deciding what a financial verification establishes.

A restoration programme becomes more convincing when published notices match the experience of customers using the affected services. That calls for clear lists of outstanding routes, updated explanations for delays and evidence that reopened services remain dependable.

The economic consequences can vary even among customers holding the same asset. Someone moving funds to a long-term wallet and a market maker relying on frequent transfers have different timing needs. Recovery quality includes predictable processing as well as the eventual return of a withdrawal button.

Binance has now supplied a concrete network count and a completion goal. The remaining question is whether the exchange can meet that goal and explain any exceptions clearly. Asset replacement and cryptographic reporting support that assessment, while actual access remains a separate result to observe.

#5143. Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Two Bitcoin addresses that had been dormant since 2010 suddenly moved $6.9 million worth of BTC on Friday, bringing two early mining rewards back into circulation after more than 16 years.

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert flagged the first transfer at 4:08 a.m. UTC on November 13, when 50 BTC worth approximately $3.44 million moved from an address that had not spent its original mining reward since September 2010.

Just over two minutes later, another 50 BTC moved from a separate wallet with an equally long history.

Both transfers involved Bitcoin originally generated through mining, rather than coins purchased on an exchange. Their combined value today was approximately $6,885,068.

The coins came from two blocks mined on September 8 and September 19, 2010, respectively. Back then, Bitcoin traded for roughly six cents, meaning each 50 BTC reward was worth about three bucks.

At Friday's transaction prices of around $68,800 per Bitcoin, their combined value had increased approximately 1,147,511 times, equivalent to a 114,751,033% increase.

That percentage measures the appreciation in Bitcoin's market price (what’s known as unrealized gains), not money the holder has actually made by selling (which would be known as realized gains). In fact, it’s unknown whether this was a peer-to-peer transaction, an OTC sell, or simply a wallet switch for security reasons.

The $3 valuation is also an estimate. Bitcoin barely had a functioning market in September 2010, with historical prices showing a trading range of around five to seven cents. The Mt. Gox exchange had only opened that July, with its first recorded trade taking place at $0.04951 per coin.

The transfers are part of a broader trend of ancient Bitcoin wallets waking up in 2026. According to Galaxy Research data highlighted in August, Bitcoin that had remained untouched for at least a decade was moving at a pace rarely seen in previous years. In one 10-day stretch alone, six wallets dating back to 2011, 2012, and 2014 transferred a combined 553.59 BTC, worth more than $40 million at the time.

Some of those movements have been linked to security concerns, wallet upgrades, or transfers to professional custodians rather than outright selling. Friday's activity adds another 100 BTC to the growing list of early Bitcoin holdings changing hands—or at least changing addresses—after more than a decade of silence.

The blockchain provides a detailed record of where the money moved, but it doesn't reveal who controls the receiving wallets.

The first transaction split the 50 BTC into two new addresses, sending nearly 49.99 BTC to one and approximately 0.01 BTC to another, minus a tiny network fee.

The second transaction followed a similar pattern, transferring nearly 49 BTC to one address and approximately 1 BTC to another.

Both transactions cost just 1,110 satoshis each in network fees, equivalent to approximately $0.75. A satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest unit, worth one hundred-millionth of a BTC.

As of an on-chain check at approximately 14:00 UTC Friday, the 100 BTC had not moved again from their new destinations following the consolidation, and no sale has been identified.

#5142. Wells Fargo Reports $2.35 Billion in BlackRock Bitcoin ETF Shares, but the Filing Needs Context

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

A new securities disclosure puts Wells Fargo among the largest reported holders of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, with a position valued at approximately $2.35 billion at the end of September. The scale is striking, but the story is not as simple as a bank buying billions of dollars of Bitcoin for itself. Form 13F reporting can include assets managed for customers, and it captures an older quarter-end rather than today’s trading. That distinction matters after Bitcoin’s sharp decline in November.

According to CoinDesk’s analysis of the filing disclosed on November 16, Wells Fargo reported about 49.58 million IBIT shares at September 30, compared with 24.4 million at the end of June. The share count therefore more than doubled. The value rose from roughly $812 million to $2.35 billion, a bigger percentage increase because the ETF also appreciated over the quarter. Reported shares and dollar valuations tell related but different stories: one indicates a change in positions, while the other incorporates market moves. A filing does not disclose each trade date, and it cannot identify which accounts made the purchases without additional information.

Wells Fargo’s investment-management reporting perimeter encompasses positions that may be held or managed for clients. It is not proof that the bank committed the entire reported amount from its own treasury. The 13F also concerns securities rather than Bitcoin held in an on-chain wallet. BlackRock’s fund holds the underlying asset; an investor in IBIT owns fund shares and gains exposure through their price. That structure is particularly important when comparing institutional reports. A large line item can reflect adviser activity, custody or delegated investment decisions rather than one central corporate allocation.

For related context, see our earlier report on JPMorgan's third-quarter bitcoin-fund disclosure.

The reported IBIT holding represents exposure to roughly 28,000 Bitcoin when scaled using the fund’s published quarter-end holdings and shares outstanding, according to the same analysis. That number should not be described as Bitcoin directly controlled by Wells Fargo. Nor does it tell us anything about whether the positions were retained during November’s sell-off. The September snapshot predates recent market weakness by weeks. Treating a delayed filing as evidence of current buying risks misreading both the timing and the investor behind the position.

There is nevertheless a useful trend here: the channels through which conventional financial institutions and their customers obtain Bitcoin exposure are expanding beyond dedicated crypto businesses. ETF shares can sit inside familiar investment operations, making reported positions easier to compare with conventional securities. The harder question is how persistent that exposure will prove when prices are falling and fund flows are negative. Fresh filings, fund creation and redemption data, and any changes in risk limits will offer a better indication than this one quarter-end snapshot.

The timing also matters for interpreting the filing. A third-quarter 13F arrives weeks after the positions it describes, and the September quarter-end share count cannot answer whether a manager bought or sold during the November drawdown. A client portfolio may be rebalanced for reasons unrelated to an institution's corporate conviction. For meaningful comparisons, analysts should check a consistent set of filing entities across quarters, rather than adding together affiliated accounts or equating changes in reported value with net purchases. That approach limits double counting and headline inflation.

For related context, see our earlier report on Harvard and Dartmouth's ETF filings.

The next disclosures will be more informative if they show how many shares remained in these reporting accounts at December 31. Until then, the figures support a statement about a large reported ETF position at September’s close, not a prediction about the next Bitcoin price move or the bank’s proprietary trading decisions.

Reporting sources: CoinDesk analysis of the newly disclosed 13F

Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab announced new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

Nvidia released a new decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the company, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia said that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing."

Nvidia and IBM also announced plans for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform."

In 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

#5140. Hong Kong’s SWIFT Push Puts XRP Back In Focus

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Hong Kong’s SWIFT Push Puts XRP Back In Focus

Programmable blockchain payments are coming: Swift is plugging its ledger into Hong Kong’s Project Ensemble.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced on 16 November, 2026 a strengthened partnership with Swift to explore how tokenised deposits can improve the speed and end-to-end experience of cross-border transactions.

The work builds on collaboration that began in 2023 through the Project Ensemble Sandbox, where the two organisations tested interoperability between central bank digital currency systems.

The latest phase brings in major Hong Kong banks, including Bank of China (Hong Kong), Standard Chartered, and HSBC, to examine how the Swift ledger can connect with Project Ensemble’s settlement layer.

The goal is to develop mechanisms that use multi-currency tokenised deposits for cross-border payments, using Swift’s global network to link international and local systems more tightly.

HKMA Deputy Chief Executive Howard Lee described it as another step toward supporting real-time, always-on, and programmable cross-border transactions.

Swift is plugging its ledger into Hong Kong's Project Ensemble.The HKMA, Swift, HSBC, Standard Chartered and Bank of China (Hong Kong) will explore moving tokenized deposits across borders in multiple currencies. The goal is real-time, 24/7, programmable payments.It's still…

Swift’s Chief Business Officer Thierry Chilosi noted that as domestic systems evolve to handle new forms of digital value, the organisation is exploring how its ledger can connect these platforms across borders so institutions can settle more efficiently.

This is not Hong Kong’s first experiment with tokenised assets and digital money infrastructure. In 2023, Ripple and Fubon Bank participated in the HKMA’s inaugural e-HKD Pilot Programme.

Their use case combined a hypothetical e-HKD with tokenised real estate (property liens) and lending protocols to enable faster access to home equity.

The solution ran on a private ledger built with the same technology as the XRP Ledger, with Ripple’s CBDC platform handling the digital currency layer.

That earlier pilot focused on domestic retail and asset-tokenisation scenarios. The new HKMA x Swift x XRP work shifts the emphasis toward wholesale interbank settlement and multi-currency cross-border flows using tokenised deposits.

Both efforts share the same underlying requirement: different systems, whether CBDC platforms, tokenized deposit ledgers, or traditional messaging networks, must be able to interoperate without forcing every participant on one rail.

Public blockchains such as the XRP Ledger have long been positioned by their proponents as neutral settlement layers that can sit between otherwise incompatible systems.

HKMA + SWIFT + tokenized deposits is a peak "TradFi meets onchain" moment 🤝 honest q fam: would you hold tokenized bank deposits, or stick with stablecoins? 🤔

XRP itself is frequently discussed as a potential bridge asset for currency conversions in corridors where no single national digital currency is suitable as an intermediary.

Ripple’s earlier work with the HKMA already demonstrated that XRPL-derived technology could support tokenized asset and CBDC-related use cases inside a regulated pilot.

The current Project Ensemble-Swift collaboration does not name any public blockchain or bridge asset. The programme focuses on connecting existing institutional infrastructure with emerging tokenised-deposit systems.

WhiteBIT has relaunched its over-the-counter (OTC) platform and enhanced its institutional offering with a large-volume trading section for digital assets and fiat currencies. It is tailored for institutional and corporate clients, investment funds, family offices, and other participants in the market that seek a special approach when having high-value deals.

Unlike normal exchange trading, where big orders may impact market prices and execution expenses, OTC trades are transactions carried out outside the public order book, straight between a client and the trading desk. This can reduce the impact on the market, give more flexibility in terms of the execution period, and give more customization for institutional trading.

“The institutional engagement with cryptocurrencies is growing at the level of more than just access to cryptocurrencies. Equipped with a reliable compliance framework, a dedicated team of support, and processes that are predictable in their operations, funds, corporate treasuries, and professional investors require execution models that allow them to operate in the same way they do in traditional financial markets. By relaunching our OTC desk, we’re strengthening the infrastructure that enables these participants to execute large transactions more efficiently and with greater flexibility,” said Volodymyr Nosov, Founder and President of W Group, of which WhiteBIT is a part.

The relaunched desk supports crypto-to-fiat and fiat-to-crypto transactions in major fiat currencies, including the US dollar (USD), euro (EUR), British pound (GBP), and Swiss franc (CHF), as well as the stablecoins USDT and USDC. Also, the top 10 crypto assets by market capitalization are now available for trading on the OTC desk against USDT and USDC. Other crypto assets outside the top 10 and additional fiat currencies are available upon individual request.

WhiteBIT does not impose a fixed upper limit on OTC transaction sizes. Instead, the maximum amount is determined by the source of funds and the results of the required compliance checks, so capacity is set around each client’s actual activity.

Each client is assigned to a dedicated OTC manager, who provides them with support in negotiating the transaction parameters, agreeing the terms of execution, and support throughout the transaction. The service protects client data and transactional information and follows Know Your Customer (KYC), Know Your Business (KYB), and all applicable compliance regulations.

WhiteBIT is introducing a zero-fee offer for new OTC clients, covering their first transaction of up to $2 million. It is a one-time offer, valid for three months from release, after which it can be extended; transactions with the top 10 crypto assets are not covered by the offer. Deals with a value of more than 2 million are processed as a single tranche with an indicative price derived from the OTC pricing strategy established in advance with the client’s dedicated OTC manager, allowing institutional and corporate clients to plan bigger deals from the beginning.

The relaunch is a part of WhiteBIT’s institutional and professional market business growth strategy. With the addition of a dedicated OTC execution channel, WhiteBIT will aim to provide crypto liquidity and allow more flexibility in handling large-scale digital asset transactions for businesses and investors.

WhiteBIT is a leading global crypto exchange by user traffic, offering over 1020 trading pairs, 370+ assets, and supporting 8 fiat currencies. With a strong focus on regulatory compliance, WhiteBIT serves 10 million users across six continents and more than 150 countries. Founded in 2018, the platform is part of W Group, which has more than 40 million customers globally. WhiteBIT collaborates with Visa, FACEIT, FC Barcelona, Juventus FC, and the Ukrainian national football team. The company is dedicated to driving the widespread adoption of blockchain technology worldwide.

#5138. Evernorth’s XRP Treasury Carries $505 Million of Write-Downs Under an Unusual Accounting Rule

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Evernorth’s first quarterly disclosure since its Nasdaq listing contains a number that demands an explanation: roughly $505 million in cumulative write-downs against XRP originally recorded at about $847 million. This is not the same as announcing that the company sold half a billion dollars of tokens at a loss. The Ripple-backed treasury business is applying an impairment model to certain holdings, and the resulting book value can sit well below their quoted market value. It is a lesson in how crypto company accounts can diverge from the assets investors think they are buying.

Evernorth reported around 346 million XRP with a carrying amount of $341.9 million at September 30. The filing shows approximately $233.7 million in impairment during 2025 and $271.0 million over the first nine months of 2026, adding to about $504.7 million. Those are noncash accounting reductions to the original recorded cost basis for the affected assets. The company’s filing also uses a September 30 Coinbase closing XRP price of about $1.49 elsewhere in its fair-value calculations. A market-price multiplication would therefore produce a different number from the historical carrying amount, illustrating why the two measures cannot be substituted for each other.

Many corporate crypto holdings now qualify for fair-value treatment that recognizes both price increases and decreases in earnings. Evernorth says its accounting relationship with Ripple means the XRP at issue does not qualify for that newer treatment. Instead, after a decline triggers an impairment, a subsequent recovery does not automatically lift the asset’s carrying value. The discrepancy is therefore partly structural. Two publicly listed firms can hold volatile digital assets while reporting dramatically different earnings patterns because the relevant accounting tests and related-party facts differ.

For related context, see our earlier report on another digital-asset treasury accounting example.

Investors should separate at least three ideas: cash spent to acquire XRP, the amount at which those tokens are currently recorded, and the market value of tokens still held. An impairment is not evidence of a wallet transfer or disposal. Equally, it should not be waved away as meaningless, because the rules shape reported net assets and future recognized gains. Evernorth also reported a roughly $33 million loss for the first nine months of 2026, supported by a substantial noncash gain elsewhere. Reading only the headline profit or loss would conceal much of that composition.

The real questions concern how the treasury is funded, whether its holdings change, what related-party restrictions remain relevant and how the accounting policy affects comparisons with other crypto-treasury companies. Investors should also examine issuance and dilution, not just the number of tokens acquired. Further quarterly reports may provide better evidence about deployment and operating results. Any claim that the write-down itself predicts XRP’s next move goes beyond what the September balance sheet can establish.

There is a further distinction between a company's token cost basis and the quoted market value of its holdings. Accounting classifications can produce different paths for recognising losses and subsequent gains, even when two firms own the same asset. Readers should look beyond the aggregated balance-sheet figure to the footnotes describing the impairment calculation, disposal assumptions and whether valuation recovery is permitted. Those policies may affect future reported earnings independently of XRP trading volumes, treasury spending or the company's commercial activity.

For related context, see our earlier report on financial-institution crypto disclosures.

The filing is most useful when read as a reconciliation between original cost, impairment and remaining token inventory. It explains the bookkeeping behind a dramatic headline without removing the economic risk of holding XRP. Shareholders still bear exposure to the token’s price, the company’s capital structure and its execution.

#5137. Harvard Refuses to Dump Bitcoin Holdings Despite Downturn

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

The Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#5136. JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan Chase, whose CEO has spent years deriding crypto, is now sitting on close to $1 billion worth of crypto-linked stocks and funds, a regulatory filing shows, after the bank deepened those positions in the third quarter.

Adding up the disclosures in JPMorgan’s quarterly 13F, the form large institutional managers must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to report their holdings, the bank held roughly $981 million across spot Bitcoin ETFs, Michael Saylor’s Strategy, and crypto exchange Coinbase as of Sept. 30.

Counting its stakes in Robinhood and Bitcoin miners, the total likely tips past $1 billion.

The largest piece is BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, or IBIT, where JPMorgan reported 11,408,930 shares worth about $540 million, a 9.6% increase in shares from the prior quarter, when the holding was valued at roughly $356 million. It held smaller positions in Grayscale’s and Bitwise’s Bitcoin ETFs, bringing its total spot Bitcoin ETF exposure to around $549 million.

The bank also leaned further into Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury company, raising its stake 36% to 848,932 shares, up from 624,387 at the end of June. That position was valued at about $131.3 million, up from $57.9 million a quarter earlier, reflecting both the added shares and a rise in Strategy’s stock over the period.

A roughly $301 million stake in Coinbase rounds out the core holdings, alongside positions in Robinhood and miners including Core Scientific and Hut 8. JPMorgan also disclosed sizable options tied to both IBIT and Strategy.

The company’s 13F is a snapshot as of Sept. 30 and doesn’t capture moves since, nor does it necessarily reflect directional bets. Banks often hold such positions to hedge or to facilitate client trades rather than to wager on price, so the near-$1 billion figure is better read as the scale of JPMorgan’s crypto-market activity than as a conviction call.

That nuance matters given CEO Jamie Dimon, who has called Bitcoin worthless and likened crypto to a fraud, even as the bank he runs steadily builds out digital-asset services.

Those services have expanded quickly. JPMorgan recently issued its first price forecast for Bitcoin, rolled out a deposit token called JPM Coin tied to bank dollars on Ethereum, and explored tokenized stocks alongside BlackRock and the DTCC.

The disclosure also lands during a rough stretch for Bitcoin funds. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled more than $1.4 billion over a recent five-day span as investors cut risk, a reminder that the institutional appetite captured in JPMorgan’s September snapshot has cooled since.

Bitcoin, which traded near $155 per Strategy share levels at quarter-end, has since slid well off its highs, today trading below $69,000.

#5134. Ripple's Schwartz Reveals Why XRP Ledger Used Satoshi's Code

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet said that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating new ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," said Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz said it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

"It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz said.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.
