#5133. Judge Acquits Brothers in $25 Million Ethereum MEV Case After Finding No Proven Wire Fraud

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

A Manhattan federal judge has acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of criminal charges stemming from a 2023 Ethereum trading maneuver that prosecutors said extracted about $25 million. The decision is important, but the takeaway needs precision. It does not amount to judicial approval of every aggressive trading technique on public blockchains. Instead, the judge found that prosecutors failed to prove the material misrepresentations necessary for wire fraud and related convictions in this particular case.

The case concerned maximal extractable value, or MEV, the ability to affect the ordering or inclusion of blockchain transactions for financial gain. Prosecutors said the brothers engineered a bait-and-switch involving Ethereum validator infrastructure and trading bots in April 2023. Their alleged manipulation diverted value that the bots otherwise expected to capture. The defense contested the fraud theory. The unusual technical setting made the case a test of how existing criminal statutes apply to blockchain transactions that may be opportunistic or adversarial but do not necessarily resemble ordinary deceptive financial communications.

US District Judge Jessica Clarke focused on whether the conduct, as charged and proved, met the legal requirements for fraud. According to the ruling reported by Reuters and The Block, the relevant transactions did not involve material false representations of the kind prosecutors needed to establish. The judge distinguished that legal test from the question of whether the behavior was fair, ethical or objectionable. She also noted the absence of a regulated-market rule prohibiting the charged conduct in that setting. An acquittal under particular charges does not pronounce on every possible theory of liability.

For related context, see our earlier report on the Kava Lend collateral exploit.

The brothers were arrested in May 2024, and a jury failed to reach a verdict in November 2025. That sequence matters when interpreting Monday’s ruling: the result followed substantial litigation rather than a quick dismissal immediately after an indictment. The court’s reasoning offers a specific limit on a criminal fraud case, not a complete set of rules for MEV markets. Other facts, jurisdictions or statutory claims could produce different outcomes. Describing the ruling as the legalization of MEV attacks would overstate what the court decided.

MEV remains a practical concern for users who trade on-chain. Transaction ordering, block building and the design of trading bots can affect execution prices and who captures value. Better routing, slippage controls and protocol-level improvements may reduce some forms of extraction, but they do not eliminate competition over transaction priority. Legal certainty matters for developers and traders, while consumer protection remains a separate operational issue. The industry will be watching how prosecutors and policymakers respond to the limits the judge identified.

A ruling on criminal liability also leaves open the technical question of how MEV infrastructure should be designed. Relays, builders and validators can change their software or operational policies, but those changes have different trade-offs for permissionlessness, censorship resistance and execution fairness. Developers can study the facts of this case without treating the acquittal as a blanket endorsement of every form of transaction manipulation. The legal finding is narrower: the government did not prove the fraudulent representation required for the charged offences on the trial record.

For related context, see our earlier report on the Clearpool token-migration safeguards.

The headline is an acquittal in a closely watched federal case, not a blanket safe harbour for exploiting counterparties. For Ethereum users, it reinforces the need to distinguish legal allegations, proven misrepresentations and the technical safeguards available during on-chain execution.

Reporting sources: Reuters reporting on the federal ruling · The Block court report

#5129. China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

Chinese developers are planning and building billions of dollars worth of AI data centers around Nvidia processors restricted by Washington, according to a Reuters investigation published Friday.

After examining more than 150 procurement notices, investment plans and corporate records, the news agency identified projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion). Many specify Nvidia's H100, H200, or H800 chips, which provide the computing power used to train and run advanced AI models.

But $3.2 billion is the total value of the projects, including buildings, electricity and other infrastructure. The documents do not establish that all the processors were obtained, or that any export laws were broken.

One proposed computing center in Fujian province is valued at 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million). Its official investment listing specifies H100 servers but is still seeking financing partners.

In Shaanxi, a state-owned engineering group won a contract linked to a 3 billion yuan center naming H100 and H200 chips. A 2.26 billion yuan project in Jilin proposes combining Nvidia hardware with Chinese processors.

Inner Mongolia has another proposed development specifying 625 H200 servers. Meanwhile, authorities in Wuxi reported that an H800 computing cluster began operating in March 2025. Operating facilities and proposed investments are not evidence of the same level of chip access.

Nvidia's processors can carry out thousands of calculations at once, making them valuable for AI training. Its widely used software also makes switching to rival systems more complicated and potentially expensive.

The United States began restricting advanced AI chip sales to China in 2022, citing national security concerns. In January 2026, the Commerce Department moved H200 export applications to case-by-case review, although sales still require licenses. H100 shipments remain more tightly restricted.

That leaves Chinese developers with a dilemma: design facilities around familiar Nvidia equipment they may struggle to acquire, or invest in alternative processors that can require software changes and additional engineering.

An IDC report cited by Reuters estimated Nvidia accounted for 34% of China's AI accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026, compared with 28% for Huawei. Those figures cover the broader chip market, not confirmed shipments of restricted models.

Chinese AI developer Z.AI has already released an image-generation model trained entirely on Huawei chips, demonstrating that competitive systems need not depend on American hardware.

Still, the new project records show how deeply Nvidia remains embedded in Chinese AI infrastructure plans. They also add pressure on U.S. officials facing congressional scrutiny over how advanced chip export rules are enforced.

Thankfully, Shiba Inu's bearish rally might be fading sooner rather than later. The price's most recent red candle wasn't followed by a surge in selling volume, which could hint at a potential reversal.

On November 14, a single daily candle took SHIB below the July bottom around $0.0000041, with the wick reaching $0.0000037. At press time, the asset is trading at $0.00000387, the lowest level on the chart since March. Selling volume that day stayed well below the late July and August spikes.

Usually, when the price hits the bottom like that, the point of previously growing demand might become a source of additional selling pressure. For SHIB, it's the July zone, where buyers stepped in last time.

If we dive inside the 4HR price chart, we can clearly see a price/volume divergence, which is a good sign for bulls. Moving averages are diverging, so a quick retrace isn't yet possible. First of all, death crosses aren't as scary as they used to be. Second, the signal is inherently lagging, so it only reflects what was already priced in. It's more of a guideline for those who are looking for an entry.

Stellar has reached a potential price bottom where it might finally find ground for a retrace. The volume is relatively low, but the main issue is the lack of foundational recovery fuel.

The key here is the crypto market recovery in general.

#5126. Gate Adds GBP and EUR Banking Support for Gate Money via OpenPayd

Home » Exchanges » Gate Adds GBP and EUR Banking Support for Gate Money via OpenPayd

The expanded integration adds virtual pound accounts and euro SEPA rails across Gate’s unified financial platform.

Cryptocurrency and financial services platform Gate has expanded its multi-year partnership with financial infrastructure provider OpenPayd to support the international rollout of Gate Money, its unified fiat, crypto, and equities account.

Under the expanded agreement, Gate is integrating OpenPayd’s British pound (GBP) account infrastructure and euro (EUR) Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) payment rails across additional corporate entities.

The expansion builds on a partnership established in 2022, when Gate began using OpenPayd’s virtual IBANs to manage and reconcile European retail and corporate payment flows.

According to the companies, the additional GBP and EUR capabilities will support Gate Money while remaining available across Gate’s broader platform, which serves more than 62 million users worldwide.

The infrastructure expansion follows the October 7, 2026 launch of Gate Money. The product brings digital assets, equities, payments and asset management together within a single account.

Users can hold, receive, transfer, pay and exchange GBP and EUR alongside digital assets, consolidating multiple financial activities within one platform.

The launch represents Gate’s expansion beyond cryptocurrency trading into broader financial services, with fiat payment infrastructure playing a central role in connecting traditional currencies and digital assets.

“Bringing assets, accounts and payments together requires fiat infrastructure that can operate across products and markets,” OpenPayd Chief Commercial Officer Lux Thiagarajah said in a statement.

Gate Founder and CEO Dr. Han said the expanded partnership provides the financial infrastructure needed to integrate Gate’s services and simplify everyday fund management and payments for its global user base.

Gate’s expansion reflects a broader push by crypto exchanges to become all-in-one financial platforms.

Coinbase opened stock and ETF trading to all US users in February, while Kraken and Bybit have expanded into tokenized equities.

Gate announced a crypto-linked Visa card in early October, that is expected to reach more than 40 markets, allowing users to spend their Gate Money balances at merchants. Its broader platform also provides access to metals, indices, forex and commodities, alongside more than 5,400 digital assets and 12,800 stocks and ETFs for trading.

For OpenPayd, the expanded agreement deepens its role in Gate’s financial services operations, strengthening its position as a provider connecting traditional banking with digital assets.

Founded in 2018, OpenPayd offers businesses a range of financial services through a single API, including embedded accounts, foreign exchange, domestic and international payments, Open Banking and stablecoin on- and off-ramps.

The company says it serves more than 1,200 businesses, including eToro, Kraken, OKX and B2C2, and processes over $360 billion in annual transaction volumes.

For London-based OpenPayd, the expanded mandate adds to a growing roster of digital asset clients—including Kraken, OKX, Bybit, eToro, and B2C2—that rely on its API for fiat on/off-ramps and stablecoin settlement.

Seamless fiat banking rails are the missing link for crypto exchanges trying to compete with traditional neobanks as everyday financial hubs. By wiring direct fiat infrastructure into their ecosystem, crypto platforms reduce reliance on third-party workarounds and make it easier for users to hold, convert, and spend traditional currencies alongside crypto and equities.

Ripple [XRP] continues to trade below the $1 psychological level since breaking below three days ago. At press time, XRP was trading at $0.94, with the decline coinciding with the largest daily liquidations since October 2025.

As per data from CryptoQuant, the amount of long liquidations exceeded short liquidations by about $44 million across three exchanges. The deltas were $21 million, $12 million, and $11 million for Binance, Bybit, and OKX, respectively.

This data showed that Binance had the largest pressure on leveraged long orders. But the spikes happened concurrently across three exchanges, implying the activity was widespread.

Such a massive long liquidation imbalance may accelerate deleveraging as the Estimated Leverage Ratio (ELR) hits a three-month low. A few days later, the ELR crashed to 0.13, the lowest level since November 2024.

These figures suggest that the volatility of the altcoin’s price action may cool off due to forced liquidations. The sharp decline in price is forcing traders to close their existing positions.

In turn, liquidation risk was reducing, signaling a potential recovery for XRP. However, the altcoin was down about 2% in the past 24 hours of writing but with a significant trading volume of $1.63 billion.

These figures imply that institutions were going bearish on the XR alongside other altcoins. Over $1.09 million was withdrawn from the XRP ETF on the 13th of November .

Therefore, the XRP ETF was showing bearish signals, though the deleveraging could mitigate the ongoing drop.

#5124. Uniswap freezes $300,000 in stranded fees, halting automatic token burns

Uniswap proposes a new bridge and declining UNI payment threshold to release roughly $300,000 in stranded X Layer fees.

Uniswap’s proposed repair for fees stranded on the X Layer network would change both the bridge used to burn UNI and the payment traders make to claim the backlog.

Uniswap Labs disclosed on Nov. 6 that protocol fees had been accruing on X Layer but could not be released, leaving the corresponding UNI unburned. Implementation reviews on Nov. 13-14 describe a higher initial UNI payment designed to reduce the windfall available to the first trader who clears that backlog.

Uniswap’s fee system relies on outside traders, known as searchers, supplying UNI in exchange for selected fee assets held in a TokenJar, a contract that collects those assets.

The payment goes toward burning UNI, and the searcher keeps the recoverable asset value above its UNI payment and execution costs.

Converting accrued fees into a completed UNI burn requires a searcher to execute the exchange and the bridge to settle it. The searcher’s net surplus is a separate return, so a release does not require Uniswap itself to buy UNI on the open market at that moment.

X Layer's governance messages use the OP Stack bridge, while token transfers use Agglayer. According to Labs, the installed relayer followed the usual OP Stack token-bridging pattern, but X Layer’s version rejects ERC-20 transfers, including UNI.

A searcher receives fee assets and supplies UNI. X Layer’s disclosed bridge mismatch interrupted the second leg; the proposed repair changes the route and payment.

Uniswap Labs said on Nov. 6 that fees accrued, but the installed OP token route prevented releases and corresponding UNI burns.

The plan uses Agglayer for UNI transfers and a declining payment. These are proposed mechanics; successful execution and settlement remain unestablished.

Accrued fees, searcher surplus and a settled UNI burn measure different things.

The failure state is Labs’ November 6 disclosure, not an independently measured November 15 balance. Repair execution is unestablished. PR parameters remain proposed and differ from the forum’s timing. Diagram widths do not encode value.

Source-bound mechanism diagram, not a quantitative allocation. Solid and dashed connectors distinguish the disclosed stalled route from the proposed route. The proposed parameters are reported from PR 167; no price curve or clearing result is calculated.

The failure state is Labs’ November 6 disclosure, not an independently measured November 15 balance. Repair execution is unestablished. PR parameters remain proposed and differ from the forum’s timing. Diagram widths do not encode value.

Proposal 95 records execution on March 8, including X Layer fee-activation actions. The proposed replacement would use X Layer’s token-transfer route to complete the burn.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The currently edited description of Uniswap protocol-fees implementation PR 167, opened Nov. 2, estimates that roughly $300,000 of fees could be swept into the jar. It warns that restarting with the existing 2,000 UNI payment could hand the accumulated assets to the first searcher at that fixed price.

Uniswap’s collection architecture requires explicit collection calls for v3 and v4 fees, so a jar’s wallet balance alone doesn't capture everything accrued in pools.

PR 167 describes an initial threshold of 80,000 UNI, a 2,000 UNI floor and a two-day half-life. Its description estimates about 10.8 days to reach the floor.

The mechanism starts with an expensive claim and reduces the required payment over time. A searcher can act when the assets it can recover justify that payment and its costs, so competition could direct more backlog value into UNI payments instead of leaving the margin created by a low fixed threshold.

The proposed schedule remains inconsistent across the published plans: the Nov. 6 forum post says roughly six days after execution, while the reviewed implementation describes about 10.8 days.

Governance would start the decay after the TokenJar points to the new releaser. Anyone could update the threshold, and searchers could bundle that update with a release.

The setter would temporarily own the releaser, returning ownership and threshold-setting control to governance on the first update at the floor. The reviewed design removes a separate reclaim function, so elapsed time alone would not restore control.

As of Nov. 15, PR 169’s combined implementation remained a draft, listing the setter and replacement releaser deployment as blockers. The releaser and setter PRs remained open, while the official deployment registry still listed X Layer’s original releaser.

For scale, Strata Terminal reported $7.8 million in UNI burns over the preceding 30 days as of Nov. 15, and 14.1 million UNI in recurring burns overall, separate from the one-time 100 million UNI treasury burn.

That recurring flow gives the proposed one-time release context, but the older $300,000 backlog estimate uses a different observation date and valuation method. A direct conversion ratio would conflate an estimated stock of fees with realized burn flows.

The proposed repair’s economic test is how much UNI the release payment ultimately sends to Ethereum’s burn address.

#5123. Mastercard Spotlights XRP Ledger After Groundbreaking Test

After an important hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore new possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI

Global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

The hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

One of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the company's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

#5122. Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.

In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

The probe gathered nearly 1,700 pages of documents and included five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market platforms about how they detect and report suspicious activity.

Chairman James Comer framed the issue around public trust. “Americans are rightly concerned about public corruption,” he said, arguing Congress “has a duty to ensure our laws adequately prevent insider trading” and prohibit officials “from profiting from nonpublic information.”

He said lawmakers must weigh “additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people’s trust in government.”

The memo’s central recommendation is that Congress consider new restrictions on federal personnel, ranging from an outright ban on trading prediction markets to narrower limits on specific contracts, such as those tied to government decisions.

Applying such rules across all branches, the committee argued, would reinforce that government employees shouldn’t financially benefit from access to nonpublic information, and would remove even the appearance of it.

The memo stressed that existing insider trading laws already apply to prediction markets. It cited the Commodity Exchange Act, as amended by the STOCK Act, which bars federal employees, members of Congress and others from trading commodity futures, options, or swaps on nonpublic information drawn from their positions.

The committee credited the platforms themselves for policing their markets, noting that most reported insider trading incidents were first detected and flagged to regulators by the platforms. It singled out Polymarket, which recently hired a former law enforcement expert and rolled out surveillance software called “PolyGraph” built with analytics firm Chainalysis, and Kalshi for strengthening their detection protocols.

The scrutiny follows a string of cases involving alleged insider trading by public officials and government employees.

A U.S. soldier was charged in April over alleged Polymarket trades tied to a military operation that resulted in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Then, in August, the CFTC fined a former White House teleprompter operator for betting on presidential speeches.

The push also lands amid broader pressure on the sector, with the CFTC moving to assert authority over prediction markets in its fight against several states, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren sets her sights on the industry as the incoming Senate Banking chair.

#5120. CFTC Makes Historic Move With Blockchain Derivatives Approval

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

On Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He said that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

Selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

For some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

The latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

#5119. Bitcoin Holds $64K After US Bank Outages, but Demand Indicators Flash Warning

Home » Crypto Market News » Bitcoin Holds $64K After US Bank Outages, but Demand Indicators Flash Warning

Calm price action masks deeply negative on-chain demand and a shrinking profit cushion for Bitcoin holders.

Bitcoin price barely reacted to widespread online banking and payment delays across major U.S. banks on Monday, though on-chain data suggests the price stability may mask underlying weakness in demand.

Bitcoin (BTC) edged down 0.2% over the past 24 hours to trade at $64,183 on Tuesday. Crypto market liquidations totaled $278.3 million over the same period—a moderate figure pointing to an absence of forced selling or panic. Bitcoin short liquidations accounted for $88.67 million, according to CoinGlass.

The muted market reaction came despite significant disruptions in traditional US banking infrastructure. According to the Associated Press, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase’s internal systems slowed transaction processing on Monday and triggered ripple effects across the wider banking network.

Customers at several major institutions, including Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Truist, and Capital One, reported delays, particularly when sending or receiving peer-to-peer transfers via Zelle involving Chase accounts.

While traditional payment rails faced bottlenecks and renewed scrutiny over centralized infrastructure, traders largely treated the incident as a temporary operational hiccup rather than a catalyst to rotate into crypto.

Beneath the calm surface, however, on-chain metrics point to persistent buyer hesitation. A report by CryptoQuant analyst MorenoDV highlights that Bitcoin’s “apparent demand” remains deeply negative.

On November 15, the 30-day reading was around -247,700 BTC, while the one-year figure stood at approximately -1.21 million BTC, with Bitcoin trading near $65,000.

The analyst says the current contraction is among the sharpest negative readings in the period analyzed, with similar levels seen in March 2025 and mid-2026. However, he cautioned that the data does not mean Bitcoin is experiencing an unprecedented collapse or that its price has found a bottom.

What stands out more is how long the weakness has lasted. The 30-day reading has remained mostly negative throughout 2026, with only a brief recovery in late August.

The one-year reading also turned negative around late May and has continued to decline. In other words, short-term improvements in demand have not lasted long enough to signal a sustained recovery.

Bitcoin’s earlier recovery toward $80,000–$85,000 did little to improve the longer-term demand trend. According to MorenoDV, this suggests the rebound lacked strong underlying demand.

The analyst cautions that apparent demand is an indirect on-chain measure, not a direct record of BTC sales or capital outflows. Negative readings have also occurred during previous price recoveries, so the metric cannot reliably predict Bitcoin’s next move.

For a stronger recovery signal, the 30-day reading would need to improve consistently, return above zero and eventually stabilize on the annual measure. Until then, persistent weak demand remains the main concern.

Another on-chain indicator reinforces the cautious outlook. Analyst Axel Adler Jr. reported that the share of Bitcoin supply in profit fell sharply to 52% (down 7% in a week), leaving the market close to an even split between coins held at a profit and those held at a loss.

Meanwhile, long-term holder (LTH) supply fell by 73,900 BTC to 16.2 million BTC, its lowest level in 90 days.

According to Adler, both declines rank among the steepest of the past year, pointing to a shrinking profit cushion and faster redistribution of Bitcoin holdings. The market is now approaching a key threshold: below 50%, more than half of the circulating supply would be held at a loss.

A similar pattern emerged in August 2026, before Bitcoin rebounded by 24%. However, Adler cautions that one historical example is not enough to suggest the same recovery will happen again.

Bitcoin’s stability amid disruptions to traditional banking may suggest resilience, but the on-chain data tells a more cautious story. Persistent negative demand, a declining share of supply in profit and falling long-term holder balances point to weakening market support and a shrinking cushion against further price declines.

#5118. Google AI agents audit Signal’s code and one major flaw stays hidden

Google DeepMind's AI agents generated 6.5 million lines of machine-checked proofs verifying security properties in Signal's code.

Google DeepMind researchers say their AI agents produced mathematical proofs linking specific security guarantees to a compiled build of Signal’s encryption library, and they put the resulting evidence online for others to check.

The Nov. 10 AlphaProof Code report describes about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code. The result concerns a particular build of libsignal, the Signal protocol’s implementation, under explicit assumptions about cryptography and the environment in which the code runs.

The authors say five people worked on the proofs over four weeks. Humans directed the work, selected reference models and reviewed the specifications that defined what the agents had to prove.

The target was an AArch64 Linux executable using libsignal-protocol v0.105.4 and SPQR v1.6.0 inside a small command-line harness. The theorems cover session initialization, sending a message, and receiving one. Key generation falls outside that verified scope.

The Google report connects the compiled executable to specified properties of PQXDH and Triple Ratchet one-to-one messaging, including forward secrecy, authentication, and post-compromise security.

These address whether earlier messages stay secret after keys are stolen, whether senders are authentic, and whether a session can regain secrecy after a compromise.

Its two proof models provide different assurances: the symbolic analysis relies on idealized cryptographic operations and collision-free executions, while the computational analysis bounds the success of classical attackers under stated cryptographic assumptions.

DeepMind’s reported process connects human-selected requirements and one executable to a machine-checked proof, with trusted assumptions still defining the result.

A checked proof establishes the stated guarantee for the specified build and model.

Author-reported proofs for a specific AArch64 Linux harness. Specifications, execution model, routine contracts and cryptographic assumptions remain trusted. No direct verification of phone apps, key generation or groups; no independent rebuild performed here.

Source-bound schematic of the reported proof workflow and trust boundary; connectors show logical dependence, not elapsed time or measured security strength.

Author-reported proofs for a specific AArch64 Linux harness. Specifications, execution model, routine contracts and cryptographic assumptions remain trusted. No direct verification of phone apps, key generation or groups; no independent rebuild performed here.

The symbolic proof establishes handshake secrecy under specified later breaks of Diffie-Hellman, but the computational proof does not cover quantum attackers. Group messaging is outside the report’s scope, and the computational model excludes multi-device state. Its bounds also stop providing a useful guarantee at sufficiently large workloads.

The results still require trust in Lean’s checking kernel, the specifications reviewed by the researchers, the AArch64 Linux model, and contracts describing selected routines.

The project’s Nov. 11 update, merged on GitHub, says ten more library routines were verified, cutting trusted routine hooks from 37 to 27. Those hooks replace execution of selected routines with assumed descriptions of their behavior.

The update retains libsignal v0.105.4 but changes the pinned executable. The newer build verifies the machine code for those ten routines instead of relying on their modeled contracts.

The project repository provides public instructions to rebuild the pinned binary and check its proofs. A Linux-only comparator checks that the theorems and their dependent definitions match trusted statements, then replays proofs in a fresh Lean kernel.

The authors also report reintroducing two previously fixed libsignal bugs and proving that the modified binaries violate their symbolic security theorem. That tests whether the specification rejects those known regressions.

The public package gives other researchers a concrete way to check the claimed connection between security requirements and executable code.

#5117. Major Crypto-Stealing Exploit in JavaScript Emerges: Zoom, CNN, HSBC Affected

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing users multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

According to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

If successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

#5116. Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.

Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT. There is no guarantee he will receive an offer or accept one. The FT said he maintains strong ties to Huang and some Nvidia directors.

Nvidia's board told Reuters it was still selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” it said.

Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded, following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a business executive suspected by U.S. officials of having Chinese intelligence ties. The company said it had no reason to believe its secrets were compromised.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones has become board chair. Analysts have also floated Nvidia data-center executive Ian Buck and AMD chief Lisa Su as possible successors, though those names are not confirmed appointments or offers.

An internal Nvidia suggestion-box post has attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supportive of Huang's reinstatement, according to Wired. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one anonymous employee wrote.

Other staff members have demanded transparency around his departure. The campaign shows Huang still has supporters inside Nvidia; it does not mean the board has opened talks to reinstate him.

Haas, 64, is a Silicon Valley-based semiconductor executive whose career spans engineering, product development and sales. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Clarkson University and worked at chip companies Tensilica and Scintera Networks before joining Nvidia in 2006.

He spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products business, then moved to Arm in 2013. At Arm, he rose from strategic alliances to chief commercial officer in 2015 and head of its intellectual-property products group in 2017, before becoming CEO in February 2022.

That appointment came as Nvidia's proposed $40 billion takeover of Arm collapsed under pressure from regulators. Haas was suddenly running a business his former employer had tried, unsuccessfully, to buy.

He steered Arm back onto the Nasdaq in September 2023 at an initial valuation of about $54.5 billion, one of the year's largest stock-market debuts. The IPO also gave Japanese owner SoftBank a way to sell shares while retaining control.

Unlike Nvidia, which primarily sells graphics processors and related computing systems, Arm licenses chip designs and computing architecture to companies including Apple, Amazon and Qualcomm, earning fees and royalties when customers use its technology. Arm-based designs are now increasingly found in cloud servers as well as phones.

Arm reported $1.44 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, up 27% from a year earlier. Royalties from data-center chips doubled, while Arm said initial commercial deliveries of its new CPU remain on track for early 2027.

Haas also sits on SoftBank's board and, since April, has served as CEO of SoftBank Group International, helping oversee its semiconductor and AI interests. A move to Nvidia would require untangling those ties, particularly because the companies are partners whose interests increasingly overlap in data-center hardware.

For Nvidia, the next leader would inherit not just its lead in AI chips, but delicate relationships with governments and customers as Washington debates tighter export restrictions on China. Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on November 17, with Kress at the helm and its permanent CEO search still underway.

#5114. Anthropic’s Claude builds custom gadget blueprints, but consistency stays hidden

Anthropic's Claude designed circuit boards, enclosures and firmware for three working gadgets assembled and tested by engineers.

Anthropic says Claude turned short gadget briefs into designs for three working prototypes, coordinating circuit boards, enclosures, and firmware that human engineers then assembled and tested.

In a Nov. 9 research post, Anthropic described a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet designed by Claude Fable 5.2, while Diode Computers built and tested the

For the speakerphone, Anthropic said Claude produced specifications and schematics, placed components on a printed circuit board, routed the copper connections, designed a 3D-printable case, wrote the device's software, and prepared a parts list. The other two devices followed a similar process.

Anthropic reports three working gadgets from linked electronics, enclosure and firmware designs. Diode engineers performed the physical work.

The demonstration joins several design disciplines, while people build and test hardware and commercial readiness remains unresolved.

Company and commercial-partner account. Three working examples do not establish a repeated-attempt success rate. Electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing and certification remain undone; devices were not designed for mass production.

Qualitative handoff diagram from Anthropic's account. Three branches identify design disciplines, then converge into human construction and testing. Device silhouettes are schematic illustrations, not engineering drawings; connector lengths encode no time or performance.

Company and commercial-partner account. Three working examples do not establish a repeated-attempt success rate. Electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing and certification remain undone; devices were not designed for mass production.

Diode supplied occasional follow-up directives, and an engineer asked whether the virtual pet would operate without a battery. Claude was not connected to test equipment or the machines that make and assemble boards, so people performed the physical construction and testing.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

According to Anthropic, Claude checked whether the speakerphone's board would fit inside its case and found that the mute switch would collide with a wall during insertion. It added an assembly step that tilted the board into place.

For the voice-assistant hub, Claude changed the enclosure's shape to shorten microphone ports. It also wrote speakerphone firmware that dimmed the LEDs as audio became louder, keeping the device within the board's designed electrical-current limit, Anthropic said.

Anthropic said Diode manufactured all three boards directly from Claude's design files, without exchanging manufacturing adjustments, and that the prototypes worked without circuitry fixes.

Anthropic said they had not undergone electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing or certification and were not designed for mass production. A functioning prototype still needs substantial engineering work before it becomes a commercially ready product.

The disclosure also provides no overall success rate across repeated end-to-end design attempts. Its three working examples show what the collaborators say they achieved, while leaving unanswered how consistently the process could deliver another usable device.

Anthropic's planned next steps include denser, faster, and more complex boards, simulation checks, and learning from measurements of finished devices. For engineers and hardware builders, that would extend the work from producing a design toward checking how it behaves once built.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

This is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake said.

According to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

#5112. 5 Tokens That Held Up Post-TGE

Home » Cryptopedia » 5 Tokens That Held Up Post-TGE

While most crypto tokens struggle to maintain their launch valuations, these five projects have demonstrated varying degrees of post-TGE price resilience.

For almost all crypto tokens, the Token Generation Event (TGE) is the best day they will ever have.

For 2026, so far only about 28% of tokens launched remained above their TGE closing price after 60 days. The median token was trading at just 0.64x its launch close.

Tokens surviving and rising in price for days, hours, and even minutes post-launch is not an easy feat. Here are five tokens that have so far avoided the typical post-TGE collapse:

Today, $1WIN is trading around $0.045, roughly 50% above its public sale price.

It is too early to compare that performance with tokens that have been trading for months or years. What makes $1WIN worth paying attention to is that its held steady in the post-TGE price rise and has a big business behind it. 1win has operated since 2016 with 100 million players and its gaming business is profitable independently of the token.

The company also plans revenue-funded open-market buybacks, while 10% of $1WIN spent through supported products will be burned. Supply is capped at one billion tokens with no additional minting.

Hyperliquid’s HYPE remains one of the clearest examples of a token that did considerably more than survive launch.

HYPE began trading in 2024 and today is hitting over $73, leaving it several multiples above its earliest market prices nearly two years later.

The underlying exchange also gives the token an economic connection to platform activity. Trading fees flow into Hyperliquid’s Assistance Fund, which acquires HYPE, with accumulated tokens subsequently burned.

That combination of product usage, revenue and token demand makes HYPE one of the stronger examples of the kind of pre-TGE traction highlighted in Decasonic’s research.

Aster launched ASTER in September 2025 as the token behind its decentralized spot and perpetuals trading platform.

Despite substantial volatility since then, ASTER was trading around $0.65. It remains well below its $2.42 all-time high, but also far above its earliest trading levels.

ASTER has not gone up in a straight line. But more than a year after launch, the token has retained a substantial part of the value created during its early growth rather than fading toward zero after TGE.

Backpack’s BP demonstrates another type of post-TGE resilience.

The token launched in March and subsequently fell as low as roughly $0.12 in May. By this month, BP had recovered to around $0.90, after reaching an all-time high of $1.66 in October.

That makes BP interesting because its strength did not come immediately after TGE. The token went through a deep early correction before rebuilding.

It also sits inside an established exchange and wallet ecosystem, with utility including trading-fee discounts, rewards, staking and access to other Backpack products.

ZAMA is trading around $0.067, approximately one-third above that public auction price.

The token also has direct utility within the Zama Protocol, where it is used to pay for encryption and decryption services and reward operators and stakers securing the network.

Stronger 2026 launches generally arrived with real usage, paying users, revenue, TVL or another measurable source of pre-TGE traction. The token was being added to something that already worked.

A strong launch can be created by hype. Holding up once the launch is over usually requires much more.

Toto Finance is a commodity-token issuer that was eyeing to create a Cardano Strategic Copper Reserve held in a U.S. warehouse and tokenized on Ethereum [ETH]. The metal would then be sold after 18 to 24 months.

The rejection was also looking to protect Cardano’s spending cap, as the copper treasury would take about half of the remaining budget.

But the move was more of a win for Cardano holders as they protected their treasury.

Our team has remediated the issue, and the malicious code is no longer being served through our website. This incident does not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices. Your private keys remain protected by your Ledger device. For more information from Optimizely: https://t.co/CxzmBxYadb

Website optimization platform Optimizely said it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Optimizely stated that the vulnerable path has now been blocked, the injected code has been removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the issue and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring users that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

According to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

The main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

XRP Ledger trading volume surged 100% as improved RLUSD order-book depth reduced modeled costs for large XRP sales.

XRP-paired trading on its native ledger nearly doubled over Nov. 9-15, but a separate comparison of the direct market for Ripple USD (RLUSD) at two dated ledgers showed a smaller execution penalty for a 100,000-XRP sale.

DefiLlama's daily data put completed Nov. 9-15 trading at $62.6 million, up 99.9% from $31.3 million during Nov. 2-8.

The measure combines XRP-paired automated market maker swaps and order-book trades. Native XRP participates directly, but repeated turnover can recycle existing inventory without establishing fresh net buying.

NOSHASHI's ledger data showed the XRP/RLUSD automated market maker holding 2.165 million RLUSD at Nov. 9's close and 1.861 million on Nov. 16, a 14% decline. Native XRP in the same pool slipped from 1.972 million to 1.959 million.

Over that interval, sampled funded RLUSD offers available to token sellers increased from about 19,392 to 111,951 RLUSD, roughly 5.77 times the earlier amount. Funded amounts measure what the offer owners could deliver and may be below the advertised size.

NOSHASHI's measurement requests at most 100 offers per side and counts funded depth within 10% of each snapshot's reference midpoint. Its ask side is the RLUSD inventory an XRP seller receives, and the figures exclude AMM reserves, do not measure all XRP liquidity, and do not imply that every sampled offer sits near the best price.

An idealized static model combined the Nov. 9 raw offers and pool state with their Nov. 16 equivalents. For each snapshot, it allocated XRP between funded offers and the constant-product pool according to which supplied more RLUSD for the next XRP sold.

The pool calculation includes its ordinary trading fee, 0.308% at the earlier ledger and 0.315% at the later one. XRPL can combine offers and AMMs in an actual transaction, but this calculation is not account-specific pathfinding or a completed fill.

The benchmark is the midpoint of the sampled book's tightest uncrossed bid and ask quotes, equivalent to about 1.098 RLUSD per XRP on Nov. 9 and 0.951 on Nov. 16.

In CryptoSlate's calculations, the shortfall for 100,000 XRP narrowed from 3.57% to 0.48% against each snapshot's own reference midpoint.

This compares modeled proceeds with the token amount implied by that reference price and includes spread, modeled AMM fees, and price impact. The lower absolute proceeds on Nov. 16 reflect XRP's lower price in RLUSD, despite the smaller relative penalty.

The smaller trades did not share that improvement: the 1,000-XRP shortfall widened from 0.05% to 0.11%, while at 10,000 XRP, it widened from 0.05% to 0.19%.

In the later snapshot, the larger modeled sale relied more heavily on funded offers. On Nov. 9, only about 17,701 XRP went to the sampled book, leaving 82,299 XRP for the pool. On Nov. 16, about 88,471 XRP went to offers and 11,529 XRP to the pool.

#5108. OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s dots complete purchases with tokenized card details, after users approve each transaction. The limited rollout targets U.S. ChatGPT Pro users; the wallet does not hold crypto or a cash balance. Coinbase and Circle offer a different route, using stablecoins to let agents pay for services with less human involvement.

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, giving its AI agents a way to purchase products using American Express, Mastercard, and Visa cards. The new system lets an agent finish online checkout without accessing the customer's actual card number, and it doesn't involve cryptocurrency.

The wallet works through dots, OpenAI's always-on AI assistants, which can browse websites and carry out tasks for users. A customer saves an eligible card, reviews the order and approves the payment using a security check such as a fingerprint or Face ID.

After approval, the card network creates a payment token containing substitute card details. The agent submits the token through the merchant’s existing checkout system, while the customer keeps applicable card rewards and dispute protections, according to OpenAI’s announcement.

“An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments,” Sherri Haymond, Mastercard's global head of digital commercialization, said in the announcement.

OpenAI previously introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe in September 2025, allowing people to buy from participating merchants inside ChatGPT. Wallet takes a different approach: agents can navigate ordinary online stores and use existing checkout forms, without requiring each business to build a special integration.

OpenAI is also courting merchants. Just three days before the Wallet launch, it introduced business profiles that let companies update product information and connect with potential customers through ChatGPT.

Google is working on a competing approach. Its Universal Commerce Protocol, introduced in January, aims to connect shopping agents with retailers, payment providers and post-purchase services across Google products.

Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets in February, giving software the ability to spend USDC, trade tokens, and pay for online services within preset limits. Unlike ChatGPT Wallet, the Coinbase product is primarily developer infrastructure, not a consumer checkout feature.

“It's not an SDK, it's not a library—it's a purpose-built wallet to work with an agent as quickly as possible,” Coinbase engineering executive Erik Reppel told Decrypt at the launch.

Coinbase's x402 protocol lets software pay for data or computing services as part of a web request, often using the USDC stablecoin. That makes tiny transactions possible without requiring an agent to enter card details or obtain human approval each time.

Stablecoin issuer Circle is pushing in the same direction. Its Agent Stack, launched in May, includes stablecoin wallets and tools for payments as small as $0.000001.

“USDC is uniquely well-suited for the agentic economy because it is internet-native, programmable, and always available,” Circle product chief Nikhil Chandhok said in a company statement.

Actual agent-driven demand is harder to measure. In September, blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs estimated that agents accounted for only 0.6% to 7.5% of filtered x402 commerce by value, using models that cannot conclusively distinguish agents from scripts.

For consumers, ChatGPT Wallet offers familiar card payments rather than a digital asset balance. OpenAI's terms say merchants remain responsible for deliveries and returns, and users must generally contact their card issuers for billing disputes.

OpenAI plans to let users authorize future purchases within spending limits or specified categories, but has not announced when that feature will arrive. In the meantime, it warns that merchant websites may block shopping agents or flag otherwise legitimate Wallet purchases as fraud.

Stellar is considering a proposal to reward XLM holders who lock tokens and contribute utility to the network. Crypto market commentator All In Crypto highlights the idea in a video reviewing Stellar’s third-quarter webinar, asking whether rising network activity can translate into stronger demand for XLM.

The proposal would put network-generated fees into an XLM rewards pool. But Dixon, speaking during the webinar, stresses that it remains an early concept open to feedback, not an approved change or a promised payout.

“I’m not sure this is the right proposal,” she says, urging participants to read the accompanying paper and explore its interactive dashboard before commenting. Her central argument is that “utility should drive XLM.”

The webinar reports that monthly payment volume on Stellar rose from roughly $1.8 billion in January to $18.5 billion in October. October’s figure was 89% higher than September’s, following eight consecutive months of growth.

Another $7.5 billion reportedly moved during November’s first 10 days. Those figures describe money moving across the network, however, not purchases of XLM or returns accruing to token holders.

All In Crypto is openly bullish but acknowledges uncertainty over the token’s future value. That distinction matters: greater use of Stellar’s infrastructure does not, by itself, establish how much additional XLM users need to hold.

The webinar also describes a U.S. Bank pilot in which the bank issued a dollar-backed stablecoin called USBDC and used it to settle a cross-border payment between its North American and European entities. Stellar’s Project Throughput offers another glimpse of its ambitions. The webinar cites early benchmarks of roughly 1.2 million payments per second on one machine and about seven million across eight machines.

Those are technology-preview results, not reported production-network throughput. The project is available on Futurenet with open-source code for developers to test.

Now, the unresolved question is less whether Stellar can process more activity than how that activity benefits XLM.

The rewards proposal could create another connection between network use and token ownership, but its design, eligibility requirements and eventual adoption remain unsettled.

#5104. A $25 million MEV ruling exposes a dangerous blind spot in Wall Street’s tokenization push

An Ethereum exploit case has brought renewed attention to transaction-ordering risks as the SEC allows tokenized stock venues to set their own safeguards.

A federal judge on Nov. 16 acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno in a $25 million Ethereum maximum extractable value (MEV) exploit case because prosecutors had failed to prove a material misrepresentation.

The decision leaves a separate question for tokenized US stock markets about what protects investors when transaction ordering works against them.

The SEC had already opened a conditional route for those markets in September on its framework, which preserves applicable securities antifraud and manipulation laws, but requires venues to disclose their policies for MEV even when they have none.

In her 46-page opinion, US District Judge Jessica Clarke found insufficient evidence to sustain wire fraud and the related wire-fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges. The missing element was a material misrepresentation in the brothers' Omakase operation.

The opinion describes a 2023 operation that used lure transactions to attract sandwich-trading bots and exploited a relay-code vulnerability, producing about $25 million in 12 seconds. The targeted bots themselves sought to profit by placing transactions around someone else's trade, a practice that can leave that trader with a worse execution price.

The case was more specific than a simple claim that someone profited from transaction ordering, since prosecutors had to establish the charged fraud.

Clarke found that the trial evidence did not establish a material misrepresentation in the Omakase strategy, and frustrating MEV-Boost's intended design could not supply that missing element.

The court also distinguished precedents involving spoofing, where orders create a misleading impression before being canceled. Here, the lure transactions executed and also were not placed on a regulated market with rules prohibiting the conduct relied upon in those precedents.

That reasoning does not establish a universal requirement that wire fraud occur on a regulated market, nor does it determine whether all forms of MEV extraction are lawful.

In a March 30 letter, the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) argued that exposing pending trades to sandwiching and front-running can conflict with securities-market expectations. It called for technical protections or fair-sequencing rules when automated market makers handle securities.

An automated market maker (AMM) lets participants trade against assets committed to a pool using software-defined pricing. The ordering of those trades can affect who receives a favorable price and who captures the resulting profit.

Keeping an investor's pending instruction private and deciding who processes it first are economically significant choices.

The SEC's Sept. 17 order created temporary, conditional relief from the definition of an exchange for qualifying tokenized National Market System stock venues using permissioned AMM pools. Certain liquidity providers trading proprietary capital received separate relief from the dealer definition until Sept. 17, 2031.

The order retains applicable securities antifraud and antimanipulation provisions, including Exchange Act Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. Its conditions include permissioned access, public notices, records, and specified trading stoppages.

A venue must describe policies and procedures designed to address it, or state that it has none. It must disclose known material risks, explain any mitigation and compensation arrangements, and describe trading-abuse monitoring or acknowledge its absence.

A venue's published account of its protections can be detailed while leaving investors exposed to risks the operator expressly acknowledges.

The SEC's public list, reviewed Nov. 16, contains four notice filers. Their submission dates range from TSV LLC's Sept. 23 notice to Formation Securities' Nov. 9 filing.

TSV LLC's current notice says Canton's architecture generally avoids broadcasting readable pending transaction contents to unrelated participants, aiming to reduce opportunities for conventional public-mempool front-running and sandwich attacks.

The operator still acknowledges risks of information leakage, sequencing, compromised infrastructure, and collusion.

OKXICE's Nov. 5 notice disclosed that it has no policies and procedures designed to address MEV. That sits alongside general protections, including permissioned participation, participant minimum-output settings, surveillance and the ability to revoke access for manipulative trading. OKXICE says those features mitigate, rather than eliminate, MEV risk.

Its planned pools use Uniswap v4 on XLayer, where the notice says the sequencer generally orders transactions according to offered network fees.

Perpetuals.com's notice proposes generally first-in, first-out sequencing, with priority for trading-halt instructions and signed arrival receipts intended to make ordering verifiable. Yet its affiliated sequencer would receive nonpublic transaction information.

A private pending-transaction route can reduce exposure to outsiders while leaving a concentrated information advantage to manage.

Its October notice describes safeguards that were not fully implemented and surveillance intended to precede trading. Formation's notice likewise describes planned safeguards for its Solana venue.

Preventing an abusive trade, detecting it afterward, and compensating its victim are different functions.

TSV says participants generally should not expect compensation for market or impermanent losses, compromised participant systems or losses caused by unaffiliated third parties, unless it expressly agrees otherwise or the law requires it.

Perpetuals.com reports no established compensation policy for the risks described in its notice. Formation specifically excludes compensation for lost or compromised private keys or wallets, which does not establish a general recovery guarantee for other losses.

Criminal proof, securities-venue duties and compensation terms address different parts of investor protection.

A disclosed safeguard is not a guarantee of prevention or repayment.

The acquittal concerns this prosecution. Venue notices include plans and operator statements, not independently tested controls. Compensation depends on the particular loss, applicable law and agreements; the graphic predicts no liability outcome.

Qualitative mapping of the court's material-misrepresentation finding, the SEC's MEV disclosure and preserved-law provisions, and disclosed venue compensation limits. Branches show distinct questions, not sequence or money flows.

The acquittal concerns this prosecution. Venue notices include plans and operator statements, not independently tested controls. Compensation depends on the particular loss, applicable law and agreements; the graphic predicts no liability outcome.

The SEC order recognizes that sequencing can support price-stabilizing activity as well as abuse. TSV says it does not intend to prevent lawful ordinary post-execution arbitrage or price alignment that avoids misuse of confidential information and other prohibited conduct.

The dividing line cannot simply be whether someone profits after another trade. Relevant distinctions include whether pending information was misused, how the venue controls ordering, what conduct it addresses, and which legal obligations apply.

The next disputed on-chain securities trade would raise questions about what representations were made, what rules applied, who controlled the information and ordering, and what recourse the investor had. Bringing stocks onto a blockchain makes those choices visible.

Nonetheless, it is important to note that the number of holders alone does not necessarily indicate an increase in unique individual investors, as existing investors could be opening new accounts.

However, each additional wallet holding SHIB tends to bolster its growing on-chain presence, positioning the asset for potential demand that could eventually bolster its price movement.

Although increases in holder count do not automatically trigger a price rally for the concerned asset, market participants expect that the new holder milestone could further drive demand for SHIB and potentially drive a relief rally for the asset following the extreme volatility facing the market.

Shiba Inu’s 1.7 million holder milestone arrived when SHIB was trading at about $0.00000382, following a 0.78% decline over the last day.

With its price trading far below local support levels, its user activity has flashed a brief bullish signal that is expected to help the asset stabilize its price movement.

#5101. What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.

Canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which launched its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.

Canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a New York company founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton launched in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.

Canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one big ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.

The network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.

In June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.

Think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.

This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.

"Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.

What sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:

Canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. New CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.

CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.

In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares launched the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.

Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.

CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.

Canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC plans to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.
