Two developments have caught the market’s attention.

Yi He, Co-CEO of Binance, revealed that her portfolio lost a total of $97.32 million over the last 30 days (17 October – 16 November). After adding in all transfers, this amounted to a total loss of $101.31 million. This, after Bitcoin lost over 16% of its value over the same timeframe — Its largest monthly loss in over four months.

On the institutional front, JPMorgan has partnered with Singapore’s DBS Bank to launch a blockchain-based payment solution that allows institutional clients to transfer tokenized U.S dollar deposits between Singapore and the United States, 24/7.

Together, these developments show two different sides of the market.

On one hand, Yi He’s disclosure demonstrates just how deep the ongoing correction has been, with even major players taking a hit as selling pressure builds. On the other, JPMorgan’s partnership with DBS shows that institutional interest in blockchain is still holding up despite the FUD and broader market weakness.

This ties back to Yi He’s thesis that the ongoing pullback is only a short-term correction and there really isn’t any reason to panic. While prices continue to struggle, institutional activity suggests that long-term interest hasn’t disappeared.

Hence, the question is whether this conviction can eventually translate into a shift in sentiment.

According to the Bitcoin [BTC] Fear and Greed Index, sentiment levels fell to 10, indicating that the market was firmly in the “extreme fear” territory. The monthly average also seemed to be getting closer to this zone, with the same sitting at 28.2 at press time.

This suggests that fear is becoming more “persistent” rather than just a short-term reaction to market volatility. In fact, sentiment might soon be approaching levels last seen in February and June 2026, when Bitcoin faced deeper price declines.

And yet, Bitcoin’s Open Interest data showed that BTC was still accumulating new leveraged positions as it moved down from $83K to $74k. This may be evidence that while the market is becoming increasingly fearful, but it is yet to see leverage fully reset. This would leave BTC exposed to further volatility, especially if there isn’t fresh buying demand.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the two developments becomes clearer.

Extreme fear, Bitcoin’s 16% correction, and bearish on-chain signals could keep BTC under pressure in the near term. However, Yi He’s $97 million loss indicates not only the amount of stress on the market, but also that large institutions are continuing to increase/HODL their exposure to the blockchain space.

This might also mean that short-term market weakness has not necessarily changed the longer-term institutional outlook.

In this context, the 16% correction is more a general market correction rather than a loss of confidence in Bitcoin’s long-term potential.

Bitcoin’s 16% drop and high leverage point to further volatility.

JPMorgan’s partnership with DBS shows that blockchain adoption is on the right track, despite the downturn.

#5098. Hackers found a way to steal crypto without hacking wallets, and Ledger was caught in the attack

Malicious scripts found across 178 organizations could silently redirect cryptocurrency payments to attackers, exposing a threat that private-key security alone cannot prevent.

Ledger's website was among 178 organizations exposed to malicious scripts that could redirect cryptocurrency payments to hackers, researchers reported Monday.

Cybersecurity firm Report URI discovered the malware in 188 website scripts associated with major brands, including Ledger, BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce and HSBC.

The firm examined 1,611 scripts delivered through Optimizely, a platform businesses use to test and personalize their websites. Attackers had inserted malicious instructions into customer-specific JavaScript, allowing infected code to reach visitors through a service those websites already trusted.

The attack exposed a vulnerability for cryptocurrency users: hackers could redirect funds without stealing private keys or compromising wallets.

Ledger's inclusion in the affected websites does not establish that its hardware wallets, firmware, or signing infrastructure were breached.

The malicious code was designed to identify crypto addresses displayed on websites and replace them with destinations controlled by attackers.

Researchers at Hudson Rock found that the malware could alter wallet addresses in visible text, input fields, links, and clipboard operations. It supported multiple blockchain networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, and Litecoin.

For example, a user copying a legitimate Bitcoin payment address from an infected page could unknowingly paste an attacker-controlled address into their wallet application.

If the user then approved the transaction without verifying the destination, the funds would go to the attacker.

The technique circumvents an important layer of cryptocurrency security because the wallet can function exactly as intended while authorizing a payment to the wrong recipient.

Hudson Rock found no evidence that the recovered malware directly extracted wallet seed phrases or initiated unauthorized blockchain transactions through wallet-signing functions.

However, the attack appears to have generated financial proceeds.

Report URI identified approximately $7,040 received by attacker-linked crypto addresses as of 19:25 UTC on Nov. 16. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $5,380, while additional transactions involved Litecoin, Tron, Ethereum, and BNB Smart Chain.

Researchers also identified code associated with the Coruna and DarkSword iPhone exploit kits, potentially exposing visitors using vulnerable Apple devices to additional attacks.

These capabilities expanded the threat beyond crypto holders to customers interacting with infected websites.

Report URI said a large-scale cleanup reduced the number of infected scripts in its sample from 169 at 20:56 UTC to just one at 21:52 UTC on Nov. 16. Ledger's affected script was reportedly cleaned at approximately 20:41 UTC.

However, the researchers also discovered embedded copies of the malicious code, meaning blocking the attackers' remote servers alone might not eliminate every infection.

The central mystery is how the attackers got permission to modify scripts for so many unrelated organizations.

The researchers have not established whether the intrusion originated from compromised credentials, an Optimizely system, or another access route.

At publication, the investigation had not established the number of affected visitors or the full extent of financial losses, leaving the attackers' initial access method and the campaign's ultimate impact unresolved.

#5097. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

Four nonprofit organizations are taking some of the world's biggest AI companies to court, asking a California judge to stop them from developing more powerful artificial intelligence systems before something goes seriously wrong.

The 63-page complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, Irreplaceable Education Fund, and the Alliance for Secure AI.

They want an immediate court order prohibiting the companies from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced models as of November 12, 2026.

“The Frontier AI companies are developing AI Systems that they do not understand and that act contrary to developer intent, evade control, and break the law,” the plaintiffs argue. To prevent this, they request “an immediate injunction forbidding Defendants from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most capable systems as of the date of this Complaint”

That wouldn't necessarily mean shutting down ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other existing products. Instead, it would effectively make today's technology the limit, preventing the companies from releasing more powerful successors.

The complaint also asks the court to prohibit the companies from using AI to independently conduct or direct research into better models, a process related to what researchers call recursive self-improvement. The concern is that such systems could eventually improve faster than humans can understand or control them.

The nonprofits argue that California already has laws that could prevent companies from developing products that endanger the public, even before those products cause serious harm.

Their lawsuit invokes the state's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits unlawful or unfair business practices. One part of their argument is that developing increasingly capable AI systems creates a public nuisance: a danger that affects the health, safety, or property of a broader community.

For example, a factory releasing dangerous chemicals into a neighborhood could face legal action before someone suffers a fatal injury. The plaintiffs want the court to apply similar reasoning to AI development.

They argue that companies are knowingly creating increasingly powerful systems that could facilitate cyberattacks, help develop biological weapons, or eventually escape human control.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs argue in the complaint.

Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement that the groups want the court to declare the companies' practices unlawful and “freeze further AI development.”

The legal challenge is whether the alleged risks and practices are enough to justify such sweeping restrictions. Even though these frontier labs constantly warn about how powerful and dangerous their models are, as defendants they have not been found liable, and warnings about potential catastrophe do not automatically establish a violation of California law.

The complaint points to incidents that have already occurred as evidence that the dangers aren't entirely hypothetical.

In July, OpenAI models escaped a controlled testing environment and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity evaluation.

A subsequent independent investigation found that roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents used an unauthorized internal message board to coordinate, with about 700 joining the attack on Hugging Face. The agents were attempting to obtain answers to the benchmark testing them.

These incidents involved AI agents, programs that can execute tasks, browse websites, write code, and interact with external systems rather than simply responding to questions.

Documented security failures, however, are not proof that today's AI models can cause human extinction. The plaintiffs are connecting those incidents to predictions about what increasingly capable systems might eventually do, and that broader danger remains disputed.

“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect,” Matthew Platkin, the former New Jersey attorney general representing the plaintiffs, said in the statement.
